Overview and the core puzzle

Biological neurons obey Dale’s principle (or Dale’s law), which constrains neurons to release the same type of neurotransmitter at all their synapses, making excitatory neurons form only excitatory connections and inhibitory neurons only inhibitory ones, and thereby disallowing sign reversal at synapses of the same type to achieve a negative postsynaptic current purely by changing the sign of synaptic efficacy in the same neuron class.<cite id="646b3cd0-3">The rule of thumb, Dale’s principle coined by Eccles et al., indicates that the same presynaptic neuron cannot possess both excitatory and inhibitory synapses; an inhibitory (excitatory) neuron can have only inhibitory (excitatory) synapses at its axon terminals</cite><cite id="646b3cd0-0">This is inconsistent with Dale's law that constrains a particular neuron to only send either excitatory or inhibitory currents; a simple solution is to remove connections between neurons with dissimilar selectivity so that the sign of the synaptic interaction is given by the sign in front of the synaptic term; in E neurons, an inhibitory synaptic current can originate from I neurons, while a negative sign in excitatory neurons is resolved by inhibitory input from I to E</cite><cite id="646b3cd0-4">Dale's law states that neurons are either excitatory or inhibitory, namely that w lj w kj ≥ 0 for all l and k; for a Hebbian rule to respect Dale's law one needs to prune a synaptic connection whenever the respective weight changes sign</cite>. By contrast, error backpropagation (BP) computes local weight updates in the direction of the negative gradient, which at nonlinear neurons requires synaptic changes of both signs across a single neuron’s inputs to reverse the effective local gradient, a form of sign reversal that would violate Dale if implemented directly at excitatory synapses.<cite id="510fa5f6-1">In the delta law, δj indicates the required changes in synaptic weights; the sign of the gradient provides the global direction for potentiation or depression</cite><cite id="510fa5f6-4">Backpropagation assumes synapses adjust in directions aligned with the descending gradient of a global error signal, yet this is incompatible with Dale's law fixing each neuron as either excitatory or inhibitory, constraining the sign of its outgoing synapses</cite><cite id="646b3cd0-2">A model of self-backpropagation under Dale’s law enforces that WijΔWij ≥ 0 (no sign change), while allowing ΔWij in a range that preserves excitatory/inhibitory identity, allowing synaptic modification without changing sign</cite>.

How biology sidesteps sign reversal: principles and mechanisms

1) Supervised/teaching signals that globally modulate local plasticity

A practical way to learn BP-like policies without violating Dale’s sign constraint is to add a local supervisory “teaching” signal that globally specifies the sign of synaptic change, then use a local Hebbian/STDP rule only for magnitude. Neuromodulators (dopamine, noradrenaline, acetylcholine) are hypothesized to provide such sign-based guidance; in spiking models, dopamine-like “error” variables can be propagated locally to hidden units to approximate BP, with decay and rate coding that makes the signal teachable without explicit weight transport.<cite id="510fa5f6-1">Substances such as dopamine, noradrenaline, and acetylcholine can reverse the polarity of local synaptic plasticity; the sign of the backpropagated gradient can serve as an effective proxy for global guidance to modulate local Hebbian updates</cite><cite id="538e5f37-1">A neuromodulator can perform the function of shared output error signals; dopaminergic firing encodes an error signal and influences plasticity by regulating local dopamine concentration; instantaneous output errors δo are replaced by filtered variables δ̇o with a decay constant, yielding biologically plausible “bio-backprop” performance comparable to standard backprop</cite>. Inhibition can be the carrier of this teaching signal: an inhibitory neuron’s synaptic input to an excitatory postsynaptic cell naturally contributes negative postsynaptic current, allowing the network to “invert” the local gradient direction for excitatory synapses by aligning them with inhibitory teaching inputs without violating Dale’s rule.<cite id="646b3cd0-0">In inhibitory neurons, fast synaptic currents obey Dale’s law and can be negative from I→I or positive from E→I; in excitatory neurons, an inhibitory synaptic current from I can originate and provide negative input while excitatory inputs remain positive, reconciling sign-reversal needs with Dale</cite><cite id="538e5f37-3">Teaching signals might be provided by sensory feedback or supervisory neural structures; supervised Hebbian learning uses a teaching signal to train the postsynaptic neuron to fire at target times, modulating plasticity beyond local spike timing</cite>.

2) Three-factor learning, eligibility traces, and feedback error learning

Biological circuits can implement three-factor learning in which synaptic eligibility (local pre–post timing) is multiplied by a global teaching signal (error or dopamine) and optionally by a local memory trace, avoiding explicit sign transport across layers. In recurrent networks, eligibility traces and feedback error signals can propagate credit assignment via recurrent inhibition and interneuron-mediated teaching, consistent with Dale because the teaching influence arrives as inhibitory inputs to excitatory populations rather than sign-reversed excitatory weights.<cite id="538e5f37-2">STDP provides eligibility and synaptic tagging/capture; three-factor learning rules with global signals offer a principled alternative to delayed rewards; E-prop shows spiking networks can learn with eligibility traces and broadcast error signals; predictive coding minimizes local prediction errors and can approximate backprop</cite><cite id="538e5f37-4">Predictive coding can approximate backprop along arbitrary computation graphs using only local information and largely Hebbian plasticity, with asymptotic convergence to exact backprop gradients without separate learning phases</cite>. In motor circuits, cerebellar and cortico-motoneuronal models map “target error” from muscle spindles or basal ganglia/dopamine onto inhibitory interneurons that teach Purkinje cells and motoneurons via negative-type teaching signals, yielding anti-Hebbian-like depression at parallel fiber→Purkinje synapses without violating Dale’s sign rule.<cite id="538e5f37-3">Models such as Kawato & Gomi (1992) and supervised Hebbian learning use error signals to minimize deviations; teaching signals can come from supervisory structures, enabling supervised control learning in biological circuits</cite>.

3) Constrained Hebbian and Oja-like rules that implement BP-like feature learning

Within Dale’s constraints, Hebbian/STDP-like rules can be stabilized to learn principal subspace features akin to gradient descent on a quadratic loss, circumventing the need for sign-reversal at excitatory synapses. Oja’s rule (and related “stabilized Hebbian” variants) constrain weight updates to preserve sign while attenuating eigencomponents of the input covariance, matching the sign-preserving gradient dynamics that arise when enforcing Dale’s law; under nonnegative activations and sign-preserving updates, such rules can converge to solutions aligned with BP in restricted regimes.<cite id="646b3cd0-2">Self-backprop under Dale’s law enforces WijΔWij ≥ 0 and constrains ΔWij within bounds that preserve excitatory/inhibitory identity, enabling learning without changing sign, with convergence analysis under sign-preserving updates</cite><cite id="510fa5f6-2">Dale’s backprop shows correspondence with Hebbian learning under non-negative activation constraints, with theoretical guarantees: if the optimal weight sign pattern is preserved, gradient-projection updates maintain sign and converge component-wise</cite>. In sensory cortical models, local decorrelation/PCA-like Hebbian learning at excitatory–interneuron–excitatory loops can yield near-BP performance for linear readouts, using inhibitory interneurons to carry negative teaching signals and excitatory synapses to change magnitude only, consistent with Dale.<cite id="538e5f37-1">Neuromodulator-driven, filtered error signals substitute for backpropagated deltas in hidden layers, enabling supervised learning with local plasticity approximating BP without explicit weight transport</cite>.

4) Predictive coding and precision-weighting as backprop-like inference with Dale-consistent teaching

Predictive coding posits that cortical hierarchies minimize local prediction errors via recurrent loops, with precision (teaching) signals weighting synaptic plasticity; when precision is provided by inhibitory feedback to excitatory layers, the effective teaching current is negative where prediction errors are positive, yielding BP-like weight changes at excitatory synapses without sign-reversal of efficacy: the sign is set by inhibitory input, and magnitude by local error, both consistent with Dale.<cite id="538e5f37-2">Predictive coding networks show that local prediction-error minimization can approximate backprop; oscillatory phase misalignment can encode error, unifying predictive coding with phase dynamics</cite><cite id="538e5f37-4">Predictive coding variants can approximate backprop on complex architectures with local, largely Hebbian plasticity and asymptotically exact gradients, requiring no separate learning phases</cite>. In cortex, layer 1/ITC interneuron feedback and apical dendritic inputs provide spatially specific precision teaching to layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons; this architecture is naturally consistent with Dale because inhibitory interneurons provide negative-type inputs, while excitatory synaptic potentiation/depression occurs within sign-preserving excitatory synapses that are gated by inhibitory “inhibitory teaching.”<cite id="538e5f37-3">Teaching signals can be provided by supervisory neural structures in control and sensory learning; supervised Hebbian learning adjusts timing and weights with target-driven supervision</cite>.

Circuit-level mechanisms consistent with Dale’s law

- Inhibitory “teaching” of excitatory synapses: The BP gradient at an excitatory synapse j→i can be positive or negative depending on local activation and loss curvature. If the teaching arrives via an inhibitory interneuron that targets i, the sign of the synaptic teaching current to i is negative when the gradient is positive, so plasticity proceeds without reversing the efficacy’s sign; instead, efficacy magnitude is scaled in the direction implied by the inhibitory current. This mechanism is consistent with Dale because the inhibitory neuron sends inhibitory inputs and excitatory neurons receive inhibitory teaching while changing only magnitude and timing-dependent eligibility.<cite id="646b3cd0-0">In I neurons, fast currents obey Dale’s law with positive E and negative I terms; in E neurons, synaptic current can originate from E neurons with a negative sign resolved by inhibitory input from I, yielding both positive and negative interactions at different neurons without violating Dale</cite><cite id="538e5f37-1">Filtered neuromodulator-like error δ̇o can serve as a local teaching signal for hidden units, providing the global direction modulated to Dale-consistent inhibitory inputs</cite>.

- Co-release and “bilingual” neurons as a loophole: While Dale’s law is a rule-of-thumb, some neurons exhibit co-release or mixed-sign synapses, effectively violating the strict sign rule. Such “bilingual” neurons can express both excitatory and inhibitory effects from the same axon, providing a direct route for sign-reversal teaching without Dale constraints, and may support more direct BP-like credit assignment in a subset of circuits.<cite id="646b3cd0-1">Recent evidence points towards co-release mechanisms that violate Dale’s assumption; a minimal “Bilingual” neuron model shows distinct dynamics and information-processing signatures when violating Dale’s principle</cite>.

- Pruning and sign enforcement in Hebbian learning: When Hebbian-like plasticity would change sign, biological systems may prune and reinsert links to preserve sign, effectively enforcing Dale while retaining only functionally useful connections. Such pruning plus eligibility mechanisms approximate BP by retaining sign-consistent synapses that best match global gradients over time.<cite id="646b3cd0-4">For Hebbian plasticity to respect Dale’s law, prune synapses whenever weights change sign; pruned links can be reinserted respecting the postsynaptic neuron’s type, with “frozen pruning” akin to receptor shuffling</cite>.

- Nonlinear activation constraints and sign-preserving updates: BP can be adapted to sign-preserving plasticity by projecting gradients onto sign-constant subspaces per weight, which yields convergence under suitable conditions; this provides a theoretical path for Dale-compliant learning where efficacy magnitudes are adjusted with inhibitory teaching setting the sign via recurrent feedback instead of efficacy sign reversal.<cite id="510fa5f6-2">Dale’s backprop and Hebbian learning correspond under nonnegative activation; with sign-preserving gradient projection, sign(W(t)) equals sign(W(0)) and convergence is guaranteed under standard assumptions</cite>.

Caveats and remaining gaps

A key constraint is that the plasticity direction at a synapse can depend on the presynaptic neuron’s type, with different synapse classes expressing Hebbian and anti-Hebbian rules; this sign diversity and lack of correlation with local features complicates exact gradient alignment but motivates composite learning rules and supervisory/gating signals to point plasticity in the right direction.<cite id="538e5f37-4">Plasticity diversity with Hebbian and anti-Hebbian rules and lack of correlation with circuit features make exact gradient alignment difficult, motivating local learning rules with supervisory signals</cite><cite id="538e5f37-2">Three-factor learning with eligibility and global signals provides a principled alternative for delayed rewards and local credit assignment in spiking networks</cite>. Moreover, many biologically plausible approximations (e.g., equilibrium/forward–backward nudging, predictive coding) require additional assumptions like separable layers, slow teaching variables, or recurrent feedback stability; empirical and modeling work shows these can match BP on nontrivial tasks, but exact equivalence without weight transport remains an open challenge.<cite id="538e5f37-2">Equilibrium propagation and predictive coding frameworks show how local learning can approximate BP under relaxed equilibria or local prediction-error minimization</cite><cite id="538e5f37-1">Bio-backprop with neuromodulator-like filtered errors achieves performance comparable to standard BP in multilayer networks, suggesting viable biological mechanisms</cite><cite id="538e5f37-4">Predictive coding variants can asymptotically approximate BP along arbitrary graphs with local, largely Hebbian plasticity</cite>. Finally, while a minority of neurons may co-release or exhibit mixed-sign synapses, most cortical systems likely rely on inhibitory teaching and sign-preserving plasticity to approximate BP within Dale’s constraints.<cite id="646b3cd0-1">Co-release mechanisms violate Dale’s dichotomy and may regulate large-scale dynamics, offering an alternative mechanism in subsets of neurons</cite>.

Putting it together: how biological neurons learn without sign reversal

Biological neurons do not need to reverse the sign of excitatory synaptic efficacy to implement BP-like learning. Instead, they combine: (i) local Hebbian/STDP eligibility and synaptic tagging with (ii) global/local teaching signals that specify the sign of plasticity, typically conveyed as inhibitory feedback to excitatory postsynapses, and (iii) recurrent network dynamics (e.g., predictive coding and feedback error loops) that propagate and integrate error information without explicit weight transport across layers.<cite id="510fa5f6-1">The sign of the global gradient can modulate local Hebbian updates to potentiate or depress synapses without requiring precise magnitude matching</cite><cite id="538e5f37-1">Neuromodulator-like filtered error signals can serve as postsynaptic teaching spikes/distal teaching for hidden units, enabling bio-backprop comparable to standard BP</cite><cite id="538e5f37-2">Eligibility traces and broadcast error signals in E-prop, and predictive coding’s local prediction-error minimization, provide biologically plausible credit assignment approximating BP</cite><cite id="538e5f37-4">Predictive coding can approximate BP on complex graphs with local Hebbian-like rules and asymptotically exact gradients, consistent with Dale-conserving inhibitory teaching</cite>. Within Dale’s constraints, Hebbian/Oja-like plasticity learns principal subspace features and can converge to BP-like solutions under nonnegative activation and sign-preserving update projections, while inhibitory interneurons provide the negative-type teaching needed to invert effective local gradients without changing synaptic efficacy sign.<cite id="646b3cd0-0">Sign-reversal needs can be satisfied by inhibitory inputs to excitatory neurons consistent with Dale, avoiding mixed-sign excitatory synapses</cite><cite id="510fa5f6-2">Sign-preserving Dale backprop aligns with Hebbian learning and guarantees convergence under sign-stable conditions</cite><cite id="538e5f37-3">Supervised Hebbian learning uses teaching signals to time and weight synapses for target reproduction, consistent with supervisory control in biological circuits</cite>.

In short, Dale’s principle does not preclude learning; it reshapes learning into a coordinated interplay of local Hebbian eligibility, inhibitory teaching, and recurrent/basal supervision that achieves BP-like solutions through sign-setting feedback and constrained plasticity rather than explicit sign reversal of excitatory synapses.<cite id="510fa5f6-4">Despite central importance of gradient-based learning, direct evidence in biological circuits is lacking; plasticity diversity and Dale’s law make sign-alignment difficult, motivating biologically plausible approximations</cite><cite id="538e5f37-4">Local predictive coding with Hebbian plasticity can approximate BP along arbitrary computation graphs, suggesting a viable biological route</cite><cite id="646b3cd0-4">Hebbian learning can enforce Dale’s sign constraints via pruning and reinsertion, preserving functionally important connectivity</cite>.

Title: Curl Descent: Non-Gradient Learning Dynamics with Sign-Diverse Plasticity
Snippet: Modern deep learning relies on backpropagation to compute high-dimensional gradients that assign credit to individual synapses by propagating error signals backward through the network [Rumelhart et al., 1986, Chinta andTweed, 2012]. This mechanism solves the credit assignment problem by assuming that each synapse can locally adapt in proportion to the negative gradient of the loss. However, despite its central role in artificial systems, direct evidence for gradient-based learning in biological neural circuits is still lacking [Lillicrap et al., 2020]. 

To reconcile this gap, many studies have proposed biologically plausible approximations to gradient descent [Richards and Kording, 2023]. These typically address concerns related to the locality of error information [Golkar et al., 2023, Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018, Bredenberg et al., 2023], separation of forward and backward passes [Guerguiev et al., 2017, Xie andSeung, 2003], and the weight transport problem [Akrout et al., 2019, Lillicrap et al., 2016]. However, a more fundamental constraint has received less attention: even if local gradient information were available, it remains unclear whether biological plasticity rules can consistently drive synapses along such a gradient. 

Backpropagation implicitly assumes a coordinated update rule in which all synapses adjust their weights in directions aligned with the descending gradient of a global error signal. Yet this assumption is incompatible with experimental observations. Synaptic plasticity in the brain is remarkably diverse, with different cell types and circuits expressing distinct, and sometimes opposing, forms of long-term potentiation and depression, including both Hebbian and anti-Hebbian rules [Abbott and Nelson, 2000]. This diversity is compounded by Dale's law [Dale, 1934], which fixes each neuron as either excitatory or inhibitory, constraining the sign of its outgoing synapses. Crucially, the local plasticity rule at a given synapse appears uncorrelated with the identity of the presynaptic neuron-whether excitatory or inhibitory-or with any other structural or physiological feature of the circuit [Citri and Malenka, 2008].

Title: Phasor Agents: Oscillatory Graphs with Three-Factor Plasticity and Sleep-Staged Learning
Snippet: Biological foundations: STDP and eligibility. The biological plausibility challenges of backpropagation are well known [Lillicrap et al., 2020]. A foundational observation from neuroscience is spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP): the direction and magnitude of synaptic change depends on the relative timing of pre-and post-synaptic spikes, with causal (pre-before-post) timing strengthening synapses and anti-causal timing weakening them [Markram et al., 1997, Bi andPoo, 1998]. Synaptic tagging and capture provides a conceptual model of "tag now, commit later" [Frey andMorris, 1997, Benna andFusi, 2016]. Three-factor learning rulessynaptic eligibility modulated by a global signal-provide a principled alternative for delayed reward settings [Frémaux and Gerstner, 2016]. Eligibility traces also appear as a computational device in RL, where they provide a local memory to bridge delayed rewards. 

Alternative learning algorithms. Equilibrium propagation (EP) showed that local learning can approximate backprop by relaxing to equilibrium, nudging outputs toward targets, and adjusting synapses via local phase differences [Scellier and Bengio, 2017]-a framework that maps naturally onto oscillator phase adjustment. Recent work also shows that EP-trained recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can be made robust in continual learning by adding explicit sleep-like replay consolidation phases, with further gains from modest awake rehearsal [Kubo et al., 2025]. E-prop demonstrated that spiking networks can learn temporal tasks with eligibility traces and broadcast error signals [Bellec et al., 2020], directly inspiring our dual-timescale eligibility design. Predictive coding networks show that local prediction-error minimization can approximate backprop [Whittington and Bogacz, 2017]; an oscillatory network where phase misalignment encodes error could unify predictive coding with phase dynamics. Hinton's forward-forward algorithm trains via contrastive local "goodness" rather than global gradients [Hinton, 2022], suggesting oscillatory cycles (positive vs. negative phase) as a potential substrate.
</snippet>

Title: A Survey of Robotics Control Based on Learning-Inspired Spiking Neural Networks
Snippet: In non-spiking neural networks, many successes in recent years can be summarized as finding ways to efficiently learn from labeled data. This type of learning, where a neural network mimics a known outcome from given data is called supervised learning (Hastie et al., 2001). A variety of different neuroscientific studies has shown that this type of learning can also be found in the human brain (Knudsen, 1994), e.g., in motor control and motor learning (Thach, 1996;Montgomery et al., 2002). But despite the extensive exploration of these topics, the exact mechanisms of supervised learning in biological neurons remain unknown. 

Accordingly, a simple way of training SNNs for robot control tasks is by providing an external training signal that adjusts the synapses in a supervised learning setting. As shown in Figure 6, when an external signal is induced into the network as a postsynaptic spike-train, the synapses can adjust their weights, for example, using learning rules such as STDP. After an initial training phase, this will cause the network to mimic the training signal with satisfactory precision. Even though this approach provides a simple, straight-forward way for training networks, it is dependent on an external controller. Especially for control tasks involving high-dimensional network inputs, this may not be feasible. 

Several models have been proposed on how this might work, either by using activity templates to be reproduced (Miall and Wolpert, 1996) or error signals to be minimized (Kawato and Gomi, 1992;Montgomery et al., 2002). In the nervous system, these teaching signals might be provided by sensory feedback or other supervisory neural structures (Carey et al., 2005). One of these models that is primarily suitable for single-layer networks is called supervised Hebbian learning (SHL). Title: Predictive Coding Approximates Backprop Along Arbitrary Computation Graphs
Snippet: A number of recent works have tried to provide biologically plausible approximations to backprop. The requirement of symmetry between the forwards and backwards weights has been questioned by Lillicrap, Cownden, Tweed, and Akerman (2016) who show that random fixed feedback weights suffice for effective learning. Recent additional work has shown that learning the backwards weights also helps (Akrout, Wilson, Humphreys, Lillicrap, & Tweed, 2019;Amit, 2019). 

A number of schemes have also been proposed to approximate backprop in a more biologically plausible manner, typically with local learning rules and/or Hebbian connectivity. These include target-prop (Lee, Zhang, Fischer, & Bengio, 2015) which approximate the backward gradients with trained inverse functions, but which fails to asymptotically compute the exact backprop gradients, and contrastive Hebbian (Scellier & Bengio, 2017;Scellier, Goyal, Binas, Mesnard, & Bengio, 2018;Seung, 2003) approaches which do exactly approximate backprop, but which require two separate learning phases and the storing of information across successive phases. There are also dendritic error theories (Guerguiev et al., 2017;Sacramento et al., 2018) which are computationally equivalent to predictive coding (Lillicrap, Santoro, Marris, Akerman, & Hinton, 2020;Whittington & Bogacz, 2019). Whittington and Bogacz (2017) showed that predictive coding can approximate backprop in MLP models, and demonstrated comparable performance on MNIST. We advance upon this work by extending the proof to arbitrary computation graphs, enabling the design of predictive coding variants of a range of standard machine learning architectures, which we show perform comparably to backprop on considerably more difficult tasks than MNIST. Our algorithm evinces asymptotic (and in practice rapid) convergence to the exact backprop gradients, does not require separate learning phases, and utilises only local information and largely Hebbian plasticity.

Overview and the core puzzle

Biological neurons obey Dale’s principle (or Dale’s law), which constrains neurons to release the same type of neurotransmitter at all their synapses, making excitatory neurons form only excitatory connections and inhibitory neurons only inhibitory ones, and thereby disallowing sign reversal at synapses of the same type to achieve a negative postsynaptic current purely by changing the sign of synaptic efficacy in the same neuron class.<cite id="646b3cd0-3">The rule of thumb, Dale’s principle coined by Eccles et al., indicates that the same presynaptic neuron cannot possess both excitatory and inhibitory synapses; an inhibitory (excitatory) neuron can have only inhibitory (excitatory) synapses at its axon terminals</cite><cite id="646b3cd0-0">This is inconsistent with Dale's law that constrains a particular neuron to only send either excitatory or inhibitory currents; a simple solution is to remove connections between neurons with dissimilar selectivity so that the sign of the synaptic interaction is given by the sign in front of the synaptic term; in E neurons, an inhibitory synaptic current can originate from I neurons, while a negative sign in excitatory neurons is resolved by inhibitory input from I to E</cite><cite id="646b3cd0-4">Dale's law states that neurons are either excitatory or inhibitory, namely that w lj w kj ≥ 0 for all l and k; for a Hebbian rule to respect Dale's law one needs to prune a synaptic connection whenever the respective weight changes sign</cite>. By contrast, error backpropagation (BP) computes local weight updates in the direction of the negative gradient, which at nonlinear neurons requires synaptic changes of both signs across a single neuron’s inputs to reverse the effective local gradient, a form of sign reversal that would violate Dale if implemented directly at excitatory synapses.<cite id="510fa5f6-1">In the delta law, δj indicates the required changes in synaptic weights; the sign of the gradient provides the global direction for potentiation or depression</cite><cite id="510fa5f6-4">Backpropagation assumes synapses adjust in directions aligned with the descending gradient of a global error signal, yet this is incompatible with Dale's law fixing each neuron as either excitatory or inhibitory, constraining the sign of its outgoing synapses</cite><cite id="646b3cd0-2">A model of self-backpropagation under Dale’s law enforces that WijΔWij ≥ 0 (no sign change), while allowing ΔWij in a range that preserves excitatory/inhibitory identity, allowing synaptic modification without changing sign</cite>.

How biology sidesteps sign reversal: principles and mechanisms

1) Supervised/teaching signals that globally modulate local plasticity

A practical way to learn BP-like policies without violating Dale’s sign constraint is to add a local supervisory “teaching” signal that globally specifies the sign of synaptic change, then use a local Hebbian/STDP rule only for magnitude. Neuromodulators (dopamine, noradrenaline, acetylcholine) are hypothesized to provide such sign-based guidance; in spiking models, dopamine-like “error” variables can be propagated locally to hidden units to approximate BP, with decay and rate coding that makes the signal teachable without explicit weight transport.<cite id="510fa5f6-1">Substances such as dopamine, noradrenaline, and acetylcholine can reverse the polarity of local synaptic plasticity; the sign of the backpropagated gradient can serve as an effective proxy for global guidance to modulate local Hebbian updates</cite><cite id="538e5f37-1">A neuromodulator can perform the function of shared output error signals; dopaminergic firing encodes an error signal and influences plasticity by regulating local dopamine concentration; instantaneous output errors δo are replaced by filtered variables δ̇o with a decay constant, yielding biologically plausible “bio-backprop” performance comparable to standard backprop</cite>. Inhibition can be the carrier of this teaching signal: an inhibitory neuron’s synaptic input to an excitatory postsynaptic cell naturally contributes negative postsynaptic current, allowing the network to “invert” the local gradient direction for excitatory synapses by aligning them with inhibitory teaching inputs without violating Dale’s rule.<cite id="646b3cd0-0">In inhibitory neurons, fast synaptic currents obey Dale’s law and can be negative from I→I or positive from E→I; in excitatory neurons, an inhibitory synaptic current from I can originate and provide negative input while excitatory inputs remain positive, reconciling sign-reversal needs with Dale</cite><cite id="538e5f37-3">Teaching signals might be provided by sensory feedback or supervisory neural structures; supervised Hebbian learning uses a teaching signal to train the postsynaptic neuron to fire at target times, modulating plasticity beyond local spike timing</cite>.

2) Three-factor learning, eligibility traces, and feedback error learning

Biological circuits can implement three-factor learning in which synaptic eligibility (local pre–post timing) is multiplied by a global teaching signal (error or dopamine) and optionally by a local memory trace, avoiding explicit sign transport across layers. In recurrent networks, eligibility traces and feedback error signals can propagate credit assignment via recurrent inhibition and interneuron-mediated teaching, consistent with Dale because the teaching influence arrives as inhibitory inputs to excitatory populations rather than sign-reversed excitatory weights.<cite id="538e5f37-2">STDP provides eligibility and synaptic tagging/capture; three-factor learning rules with global signals offer a principled alternative to delayed rewards; E-prop shows spiking networks can learn with eligibility traces and broadcast error signals; predictive coding minimizes local prediction errors and can approximate backprop</cite><cite id="538e5f37-4">Predictive coding can approximate backprop along arbitrary computation graphs using only local information and largely Hebbian plasticity, with asymptotic convergence to exact backprop gradients without separate learning phases</cite>. In motor circuits, cerebellar and cortico-motoneuronal models map “target error” from muscle spindles or basal ganglia/dopamine onto inhibitory interneurons that teach Purkinje cells and motoneurons via negative-type teaching signals, yielding anti-Hebbian-like depression at parallel fiber→Purkinje synapses without violating Dale’s sign rule.<cite id="538e5f37-3">Models such as Kawato & Gomi (1992) and supervised Hebbian learning use error signals to minimize deviations; teaching signals can come from supervisory structures, enabling supervised control learning in biological circuits</cite>.

3) Constrained Hebbian and Oja-like rules that implement BP-like feature learning

Within Dale’s constraints, Hebbian/STDP-like rules can be stabilized to learn principal subspace features akin to gradient descent on a quadratic loss, circumventing the need for sign-reversal at excitatory synapses. Oja’s rule (and related “stabilized Hebbian” variants) constrain weight updates to preserve sign while attenuating eigencomponents of the input covariance, matching the sign-preserving gradient dynamics that arise when enforcing Dale’s law; under nonnegative activations and sign-preserving updates, such rules can converge to solutions aligned with BP in restricted regimes.<cite id="646b3cd0-2">Self-backprop under Dale’s law enforces WijΔWij ≥ 0 and constrains ΔWij within bounds that preserve excitatory/inhibitory identity, enabling learning without changing sign, with convergence analysis under sign-preserving updates</cite><cite id="510fa5f6-2">Dale’s backprop shows correspondence with Hebbian learning under non-negative activation constraints, with theoretical guarantees: if the optimal weight sign pattern is preserved, gradient-projection updates maintain sign and converge component-wise</cite>. In sensory cortical models, local decorrelation/PCA-like Hebbian learning at excitatory–interneuron–excitatory loops can yield near-BP performance for linear readouts, using inhibitory interneurons to carry negative teaching signals and excitatory synapses to change magnitude only, consistent with Dale.<cite id="538e5f37-1">Neuromodulator-driven, filtered error signals substitute for backpropagated deltas in hidden layers, enabling supervised learning with local plasticity approximating BP without explicit weight transport</cite>.

4) Predictive coding and precision-weighting as backprop-like inference with Dale-consistent teaching

Predictive coding posits that cortical hierarchies minimize local prediction errors via recurrent loops, with precision (teaching) signals weighting synaptic plasticity; when precision is provided by inhibitory feedback to excitatory layers, the effective teaching current is negative where prediction errors are positive, yielding BP-like weight changes at excitatory synapses without sign-reversal of efficacy: the sign is set by inhibitory input, and magnitude by local error, both consistent with Dale.<cite id="538e5f37-2">Predictive coding networks show that local prediction-error minimization can approximate backprop; oscillatory phase misalignment can encode error, unifying predictive coding with phase dynamics</cite><cite id="538e5f37-4">Predictive coding variants can approximate backprop on complex architectures with local, largely Hebbian plasticity and asymptotically exact gradients, requiring no separate learning phases</cite>. In cortex, layer 1/ITC interneuron feedback and apical dendritic inputs provide spatially specific precision teaching to layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons; this architecture is naturally consistent with Dale because inhibitory interneurons provide negative-type inputs, while excitatory synaptic potentiation/depression occurs within sign-preserving excitatory synapses that are gated by inhibitory “inhibitory teaching.”<cite id="538e5f37-3">Teaching signals can be provided by supervisory neural structures in control and sensory learning; supervised Hebbian learning adjusts timing and weights with target-driven supervision</cite>.

Circuit-level mechanisms consistent with Dale’s law

- Inhibitory “teaching” of excitatory synapses: The BP gradient at an excitatory synapse j→i can be positive or negative depending on local activation and loss curvature. If the teaching arrives via an inhibitory interneuron that targets i, the sign of the synaptic teaching current to i is negative when the gradient is positive, so plasticity proceeds without reversing the efficacy’s sign; instead, efficacy magnitude is scaled in the direction implied by the inhibitory current. This mechanism is consistent with Dale because the inhibitory neuron sends inhibitory inputs and excitatory neurons receive inhibitory teaching while changing only magnitude and timing-dependent eligibility.<cite id="646b3cd0-0">In I neurons, fast currents obey Dale’s law with positive E and negative I terms; in E neurons, synaptic current can originate from E neurons with a negative sign resolved by inhibitory input from I, yielding both positive and negative interactions at different neurons without violating Dale</cite><cite id="538e5f37-1">Filtered neuromodulator-like error δ̇o can serve as a local teaching signal for hidden units, providing the global direction modulated to Dale-consistent inhibitory inputs</cite>.

- Co-release and “bilingual” neurons as a loophole: While Dale’s law is a rule-of-thumb, some neurons exhibit co-release or mixed-sign synapses, effectively violating the strict sign rule. Such “bilingual” neurons can express both excitatory and inhibitory effects from the same axon, providing a direct route for sign-reversal teaching without Dale constraints, and may support more direct BP-like credit assignment in a subset of circuits.<cite id="646b3cd0-1">Recent evidence points towards co-release mechanisms that violate Dale’s assumption; a minimal “Bilingual” neuron model shows distinct dynamics and information-processing signatures when violating Dale’s principle</cite>.

- Pruning and sign enforcement in Hebbian learning: When Hebbian-like plasticity would change sign, biological systems may prune and reinsert links to preserve sign, effectively enforcing Dale while retaining only functionally useful connections. Such pruning plus eligibility mechanisms approximate BP by retaining sign-consistent synapses that best match global gradients over time.<cite id="646b3cd0-4">For Hebbian plasticity to respect Dale’s law, prune synapses whenever weights change sign; pruned links can be reinserted respecting the postsynaptic neuron’s type, with “frozen pruning” akin to receptor shuffling</cite>.

- Nonlinear activation constraints and sign-preserving updates: BP can be adapted to sign-preserving plasticity by projecting gradients onto sign-constant subspaces per weight, which yields convergence under suitable conditions; this provides a theoretical path for Dale-compliant learning where efficacy magnitudes are adjusted with inhibitory teaching setting the sign via recurrent feedback instead of efficacy sign reversal.<cite id="510fa5f6-2">Dale’s backprop and Hebbian learning correspond under nonnegative activation; with sign-preserving gradient projection, sign(W(t)) equals sign(W(0)) and convergence is guaranteed under standard assumptions</cite>.

Caveats and remaining gaps

A key constraint is that the plasticity direction at a synapse can depend on the presynaptic neuron’s type, with different synapse classes expressing Hebbian and anti-Hebbian rules; this sign diversity and lack of correlation with local features complicates exact gradient alignment but motivates composite learning rules and supervisory/gating signals to point plasticity in the right direction.<cite id="538e5f37-4">Plasticity diversity with Hebbian and anti-Hebbian rules and lack of correlation with circuit features make exact gradient alignment difficult, motivating local learning rules with supervisory signals</cite><cite id="538e5f37-2">Three-factor learning with eligibility and global signals provides a principled alternative for delayed rewards and local credit assignment in spiking networks</cite>. Moreover, many biologically plausible approximations (e.g., equilibrium/forward–backward nudging, predictive coding) require additional assumptions like separable layers, slow teaching variables, or recurrent feedback stability; empirical and modeling work shows these can match BP on nontrivial tasks, but exact equivalence without weight transport remains an open challenge.<cite id="538e5f37-2">Equilibrium propagation and predictive coding frameworks show how local learning can approximate BP under relaxed equilibria or local prediction-error minimization</cite><cite id="538e5f37-1">Bio-backprop with neuromodulator-like filtered errors achieves performance comparable to standard BP in multilayer networks, suggesting viable biological mechanisms</cite><cite id="538e5f37-4">Predictive coding variants can asymptotically approximate BP along arbitrary graphs with local, largely Hebbian plasticity</cite>. Finally, while a minority of neurons may co-release or exhibit mixed-sign synapses, most cortical systems likely rely on inhibitory teaching and sign-preserving plasticity to approximate BP within Dale’s constraints.<cite id="646b3cd0-1">Co-release mechanisms violate Dale’s dichotomy and may regulate large-scale dynamics, offering an alternative mechanism in subsets of neurons</cite>.

Putting it together: how biological neurons learn without sign reversal

Biological neurons do not need to reverse the sign of excitatory synaptic efficacy to implement BP-like learning. Instead, they combine: (i) local Hebbian/STDP eligibility and synaptic tagging with (ii) global/local teaching signals that specify the sign of plasticity, typically conveyed as inhibitory feedback to excitatory postsynapses, and (iii) recurrent network dynamics (e.g., predictive coding and feedback error loops) that propagate and integrate error information without explicit weight transport across layers.<cite id="510fa5f6-1">The sign of the global gradient can modulate local Hebbian updates to potentiate or depress synapses without requiring precise magnitude matching</cite><cite id="538e5f37-1">Neuromodulator-like filtered error signals can serve as postsynaptic teaching spikes/distal teaching for hidden units, enabling bio-backprop comparable to standard BP</cite><cite id="538e5f37-2">Eligibility traces and broadcast error signals in E-prop, and predictive coding’s local prediction-error minimization, provide biologically plausible credit assignment approximating BP</cite><cite id="538e5f37-4">Predictive coding can approximate BP on complex graphs with local Hebbian-like rules and asymptotically exact gradients, consistent with Dale-conserving inhibitory teaching</cite>. Within Dale’s constraints, Hebbian/Oja-like plasticity learns principal subspace features and can converge to BP-like solutions under nonnegative activation and sign-preserving update projections, while inhibitory interneurons provide the negative-type teaching needed to invert effective local gradients without changing synaptic efficacy sign.<cite id="646b3cd0-0">Sign-reversal needs can be satisfied by inhibitory inputs to excitatory neurons consistent with Dale, avoiding mixed-sign excitatory synapses</cite><cite id="510fa5f6-2">Sign-preserving Dale backprop aligns with Hebbian learning and guarantees convergence under sign-stable conditions</cite><cite id="538e5f37-3">Supervised Hebbian learning uses teaching signals to time and weight synapses for target reproduction, consistent with supervisory control in biological circuits</cite>.

Title: Collective Dynamics in Spiking Neural Networks Beyond Dale's Principle
Snippet: Dale's Principle has historically guided neuroscience research as a valuable rule of thumb, namely that all synapses on each neuron release the same set of neurotransmitters. Most existing Spiking Neuron Network models share this dichotomous assumption that neurons are either excitatory or inhibitory; however, recent experimental evidence points towards co-release mechanisms that violate this assumption. Here, we introduce a minimal model of"Bilingual"neurons violating Dale's principle that can exert both excitatory and inhibitory effects. We identify parameter regimes in which this architecture exhibits transitions between synchronous and asynchronous dynamics that differ quantitatively from those observed in a matched monolingual control architecture. We report distinct information-processing signatures both at the level of neurons and higher-order interactions between them near the phase transitions. These results suggest that the population of neurons violating Dales principle may provide an alternative mechanism for regulating large-scale oscillatory activity in neural circuits.

For a Hebbian plasticity rule like (2) to respect Dale's law one needs to prune a synaptic connection whenever the respective w ij changes sign. We do this every 1000 ms of mathematical simulation time, reinserting the pruned link with a weight corresponding to 10% of the correspondingly average excitatory or inhibitory links. 

Performing test runs where the pruned links were reinserted with a strength of 1% of the average mean yielded nearly identical results. For the reinsertion process the postsynaptic neuron i is connected to a random and previously unconnected presynaptic neuron m, with the sign of the new link w im respecting Dale's law. There are two possible versions. 

Annealed pruning. Links may change sign when the new presynaptic neuron m is selected freely. The overall number of excitatory and inhibitory links may then drift over the course of the simulation, with only the total connectivity remaining constant. 

Frozen pruning. Links do not change in character when the new presynaptic neuron m is selected only among those neurons which are of the same type as j. Frozen pruning would correspond from a biological perspective to a separate reshuffling of Gaba and Glutamate receptors. 

For the results presented here we considered frozen pruning.

Title: Hebbian Learning with Global Direction
Snippet: Inspired by biological systems, where various neuromodulators can reverse the polarity of local synaptic plasticity, we conceptualize global guidance m in the GHL framework as sign-based information. In biological neural networks, substances such as dopamine, noradrenaline, and acetylcholine, serve this modulatory function, but they are generated and transmitted through complex biological mechanisms. As no direct analog for such feedback currently exists in artificial neural networks, we employ the sign of the backpropagated gradient as an effective proxy for this global signal. 

In the end-to-end training of neural networks, the global error stems from the discrepancy between network outputs and groundtruth labels, quantified by a loss function L(y, ŷ). Accordingly, the global guidance m in our framework is derived from the gradient of this global loss, ∇wL. The final weight update rule for a connection from a presynaptic neuron i to a postsynaptic neuron k can be precisely formulated as: 

where ∆w SWTA ik is the local Hebbian update which provides the update's magnitude, modulated by the sign of the global gradient signal ∂L/∂w ik . 

In our GHL framework, the primary update is computed by the local Hebbian rule, while the sign-based gradient signal serves only as a modulatory factor, indicating whether synaptic changes should be potentiated (positive) or depressed (negative). The use of the gradient's sign shares similarities with SignSGD [26,27], which is primarily designed to reduce communication overhead. However, GHL differs fundamentally in terms of update magnitude. Specifically, GHL uses local Hebbian rules to dynamically adjust update magnitudes, avoiding the instability of fixed-step updates. While SignSGD often relies on high-precision internal computations and error compensation mechanisms to recover the original gradient information, GHL only uses the directional information (i.e., the sign) from the gradient, without requiring its precise magnitude. 

The final network training procedure is detailed in Algorithm 1.

Title: Curl Descent: Non-Gradient Learning Dynamics with Sign-Diverse Plasticity
Snippet: Modern deep learning relies on backpropagation to compute high-dimensional gradients that assign credit to individual synapses by propagating error signals backward through the network [Rumelhart et al., 1986, Chinta andTweed, 2012]. This mechanism solves the credit assignment problem by assuming that each synapse can locally adapt in proportion to the negative gradient of the loss. However, despite its central role in artificial systems, direct evidence for gradient-based learning in biological neural circuits is still lacking [Lillicrap et al., 2020]. 

To reconcile this gap, many studies have proposed biologically plausible approximations to gradient descent [Richards and Kording, 2023]. These typically address concerns related to the locality of error information [Golkar et al., 2023, Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018, Bredenberg et al., 2023], separation of forward and backward passes [Guerguiev et al., 2017, Xie andSeung, 2003], and the weight transport problem [Akrout et al., 2019, Lillicrap et al., 2016]. However, a more fundamental constraint has received less attention: even if local gradient information were available, it remains unclear whether biological plasticity rules can consistently drive synapses along such a gradient. 

Backpropagation implicitly assumes a coordinated update rule in which all synapses adjust their weights in directions aligned with the descending gradient of a global error signal. Yet this assumption is incompatible with experimental observations. Synaptic plasticity in the brain is remarkably diverse, with different cell types and circuits expressing distinct, and sometimes opposing, forms of long-term potentiation and depression, including both Hebbian and anti-Hebbian rules [Abbott and Nelson, 2000]. This diversity is compounded by Dale's law [Dale, 1934], which fixes each neuron as either excitatory or inhibitory, constraining the sign of its outgoing synapses. Crucially, the local plasticity rule at a given synapse appears uncorrelated with the identity of the presynaptic neuron-whether excitatory or inhibitory-or with any other structural or physiological feature of the circuit [Citri and Malenka, 2008].

snippet.text:
Modern deep learning relies on backpropagation to compute high-dimensional gradients that assign credit to individual synapses by propagating error signals backward through the network [Rumelhart et al., 1986, Chinta andTweed, 2012]. This mechanism solves the credit assignment problem by assuming that each synapse can locally adapt in proportion to the negative gradient of the loss. However, despite its central role in artificial systems, direct evidence for gradient-based learning in biological neural circuits is still lacking [Lillicrap et al., 2020]. 

To reconcile this gap, many studies have proposed biologically plausible approximations to gradient descent [Richards and Kording, 2023]. These typically address concerns related to the locality of error information [Golkar et al., 2023, Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018, Bredenberg et al., 2023], separation of forward and backward passes [Guerguiev et al., 2017, Xie andSeung, 2003], and the weight transport problem [Akrout et al., 2019, Lillicrap et al., 2016]. However, a more fundamental constraint has received less attention: even if local gradient information were available, it remains unclear whether biological plasticity rules can consistently drive synapses along such a gradient. 

Backpropagation implicitly assumes a coordinated update rule in which all synapses adjust their weights in directions aligned with the descending gradient of a global error signal. Yet this assumption is incompatible with experimental observations. Synaptic plasticity in the brain is remarkably diverse, with different cell types and circuits expressing distinct, and sometimes opposing, forms of long-term potentiation and depression, including both Hebbian and anti-Hebbian rules [Abbott and Nelson, 2000]. This diversity is compounded by Dale's law [Dale, 1934], which fixes each neuron as either excitatory or inhibitory, constraining the sign of its outgoing synapses. Crucially, the local plasticity rule at a given synapse appears uncorrelated with the identity of the presynaptic neuron-whether excitatory or inhibitory-or with any other structural or physiological feature of the circuit [Citri and Malenka, 2008].

documents.title: Hebbian Learning with Global Direction
documents.snippet:
Inspired by biological systems, where various neuromodulators can reverse the polarity of local synaptic plasticity, we conceptualize global guidance m in the GHL framework as sign-based information. In biological neural networks, substances such as dopamine, noradrenaline, and acetylcholine, serve this modulatory function, but they are generated and transmitted through complex biological mechanisms. As no direct analog for such feedback currently exists in artificial neural networks, we employ the sign of the backpropagated gradient as an effective proxy for this global signal. 

In the end-to-end training of neural networks, the global error stems from the discrepancy between network outputs and groundtruth labels, quantified by a loss function L(y, ŷ). Accordingly, the global guidance m in our framework is derived from the gradient of this global loss, ∇wL. The final weight update rule for a connection from a presynaptic neuron i to a postsynaptic neuron k can be precisely formulated as: 

where ∆w SWTA ik is the local Hebbian update which provides the update's magnitude, modulated by the sign of the global gradient signal ∂L/∂w ik . 

In our GHL framework, the primary update is computed by the local Hebbian rule, while the sign-based gradient signal serves only as a modulatory factor, indicating whether synaptic changes should be potentiated (positive) or depressed (negative). The use of the gradient's sign shares similarities with SignSGD [26,27], which is primarily designed to reduce communication overhead. However, GHL differs fundamentally in terms of update magnitude. Specifically, GHL uses local Hebbian rules to dynamically adjust update magnitudes, avoiding the instability of fixed-step updates. While SignSGD often relies on high-precision internal computations and error compensation mechanisms to recover the original gradient information, GHL only uses the directional information (i.e., the sign) from the gradient, without requiring its precise magnitude. 

The final network training procedure is detailed in Algorithm 1.

Title: Phasor Agents: Oscillatory Graphs with Three-Factor Plasticity and Sleep-Staged Learning
Snippet: Biological foundations: STDP and eligibility. The biological plausibility challenges of backpropagation are well known [Lillicrap et al., 2020]. A foundational observation from neuroscience is spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP): the direction and magnitude of synaptic change depends on the relative timing of pre-and post-synaptic spikes, with causal (pre-before-post) timing strengthening synapses and anti-causal timing weakening them [Markram et al., 1997, Bi andPoo, 1998]. Synaptic tagging and capture provides a conceptual model of "tag now, commit later" [Frey andMorris, 1997, Benna andFusi, 2016]. Three-factor learning rulessynaptic eligibility modulated by a global signal-provide a principled alternative for delayed reward settings [Frémaux and Gerstner, 2016]. Eligibility traces also appear as a computational device in RL, where they provide a local memory to bridge delayed rewards. 

Alternative learning algorithms. Equilibrium propagation (EP) showed that local learning can approximate backprop by relaxing to equilibrium, nudging outputs toward targets, and adjusting synapses via local phase differences [Scellier and Bengio, 2017]-a framework that maps naturally onto oscillator phase adjustment. Recent work also shows that EP-trained recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can be made robust in continual learning by adding explicit sleep-like replay consolidation phases, with further gains from modest awake rehearsal [Kubo et al., 2025]. E-prop demonstrated that spiking networks can learn temporal tasks with eligibility traces and broadcast error signals [Bellec et al., 2020], directly inspiring our dual-timescale eligibility design. Predictive coding networks show that local prediction-error minimization can approximate backprop [Whittington and Bogacz, 2017]; an oscillatory network where phase misalignment encodes error could unify predictive coding with phase dynamics. Hinton's forward-forward algorithm trains via contrastive local "goodness" rather than global gradients [Hinton, 2022], suggesting oscillatory cycles (positive vs. negative phase) as a potential substrate.

Title: A Survey of Robotics Control Based on Learning-Inspired Spiking Neural Networks
Snippet: In non-spiking neural networks, many successes in recent years can be summarized as finding ways to efficiently learn from labeled data. This type of learning, where a neural network mimics a known outcome from given data is called supervised learning (Hastie et al., 2001). A variety of different neuroscientific studies has shown that this type of learning can also be found in the human brain (Knudsen, 1994), e.g., in motor control and motor learning (Thach, 1996;Montgomery et al., 2002). But despite the extensive exploration of these topics, the exact mechanisms of supervised learning in biological neurons remain unknown. 

Accordingly, a simple way of training SNNs for robot control tasks is by providing an external training signal that adjusts the synapses in a supervised learning setting. As shown in Figure 6, when an external signal is induced into the network as a postsynaptic spike-train, the synapses can adjust their weights, for example, using learning rules such as STDP. After an initial training phase, this will cause the network to mimic the training signal with satisfactory precision. Even though this approach provides a simple, straight-forward way for training networks, it is dependent on an external controller. Especially for control tasks involving high-dimensional network inputs, this may not be feasible. 

Several models have been proposed on how this might work, either by using activity templates to be reproduced (Miall and Wolpert, 1996) or error signals to be minimized (Kawato and Gomi, 1992;Montgomery et al., 2002). In the nervous system, these teaching signals might be provided by sensory feedback or other supervisory neural structures (Carey et al., 2005). One of these models that is primarily suitable for single-layer networks is called supervised Hebbian learning (SHL). Title: Predictive Coding Approximates Backprop Along Arbitrary Computation Graphs
Snippet: A number of recent works have tried to provide biologically plausible approximations to backprop. The requirement of symmetry between the forwards and backwards weights has been questioned by Lillicrap, Cownden, Tweed, and Akerman (2016) who show that random fixed feedback weights suffice for effective learning. Recent additional work has shown that learning the backwards weights also helps (Akrout, Wilson, Humphreys, Lillicrap, & Tweed, 2019;Amit, 2019). 

A number of schemes have also been proposed to approximate backprop in a more biologically plausible manner, typically with local learning rules and/or Hebbian connectivity. These include target-prop (Lee, Zhang, Fischer, & Bengio, 2015) which approximate the backward gradients with trained inverse functions, but which fails to asymptotically compute the exact backprop gradients, and contrastive Hebbian (Scellier & Bengio, 2017;Scellier, Goyal, Binas, Mesnard, & Bengio, 2018;Seung, 2003) approaches which do exactly approximate backprop, but which require two separate learning phases and the storing of information across successive phases. There are also dendritic error theories (Guerguiev et al., 2017;Sacramento et al., 2018) which are computationally equivalent to predictive coding (Lillicrap, Santoro, Marris, Akerman, & Hinton, 2020;Whittington & Bogacz, 2019). Whittington and Bogacz (2017) showed that predictive coding can approximate backprop in MLP models, and demonstrated comparable performance on MNIST. We advance upon this work by extending the proof to arbitrary computation graphs, enabling the design of predictive coding variants of a range of standard machine learning architectures, which we show perform comparably to backprop on considerably more difficult tasks than MNIST. Our algorithm evinces asymptotic (and in practice rapid) convergence to the exact backprop gradients, does not require separate learning phases, and utilises only local information and largely Hebbian plasticity.

documents.title: Phasor Agents: Oscillatory Graphs with Three-Factor Plasticity and Sleep-Staged Learning
documents.snippet:
Biological foundations: STDP and eligibility. The biological plausibility challenges of backpropagation are well known [Lillicrap et al., 2020]. A foundational observation from neuroscience is spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP): the direction and magnitude of synaptic change depends on the relative timing of pre-and post-synaptic spikes, with causal (pre-before-post) timing strengthening synapses and anti-causal timing weakening them [Markram et al., 1997, Bi andPoo, 1998]. Synaptic tagging and capture provides a conceptual model of "tag now, commit later" [Frey andMorris, 1997, Benna andFusi, 2016]. Three-factor learning rulessynaptic eligibility modulated by a global signal-provide a principled alternative for delayed reward settings [Frémaux and Gerstner, 2016]. Eligibility traces also appear as a computational device in RL, where they provide a local memory to bridge delayed rewards. 

Alternative learning algorithms. Equilibrium propagation (EP) showed that local learning can approximate backprop by relaxing to equilibrium, nudging outputs toward targets, and adjusting synapses via local phase differences [Scellier and Bengio, 2017]-a framework that maps naturally onto oscillator phase adjustment. Recent work also shows that EP-trained recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can be made robust in continual learning by adding explicit sleep-like replay consolidation phases, with further gains from modest awake rehearsal [Kubo et al., 2025]. E-prop demonstrated that spiking networks can learn temporal tasks with eligibility traces and broadcast error signals [Bellec et al., 2020], directly inspiring our dual-timescale eligibility design. Predictive coding networks show that local prediction-error minimization can approximate backprop [Whittington and Bogacz, 2017]; an oscillatory network where phase misalignment encodes error could unify predictive coding with phase dynamics. Hinton's forward-forward algorithm trains via contrastive local "goodness" rather than global gradients [Hinton, 2022], suggesting oscillatory cycles (positive vs. negative phase) as a potential substrate.

documents.title: A Survey of Robotics Control Based on Learning-Inspired Spiking Neural Networks
documents.snippet:
In non-spiking neural networks, many successes in recent years can be summarized as finding ways to efficiently learn from labeled data. This type of learning, where a neural network mimics a known outcome from given data is called supervised learning (Hastie et al., 2001). A variety of different neuroscientific studies has shown that this type of learning can also be found in the human brain (Knudsen, 1994), e.g., in motor control and motor learning (Thach, 1996;Montgomery et al., 2002). But despite the extensive exploration of these topics, the exact mechanisms of supervised learning in biological neurons remain unknown. 

Accordingly, a simple way of training SNNs for robot control tasks is by providing an external training signal that adjusts the synapses in a supervised learning setting. As shown in Figure 6, when an external signal is induced into the network as a postsynaptic spike-train, the synapses can adjust their weights, for example, using learning rules such as STDP. After an initial training phase, this will cause the network to mimic the training signal with satisfactory precision. Even though this approach provides a simple, straight-forward way for training networks, it is dependent on an external controller. Especially for control tasks involving high-dimensional network inputs, this may not be feasible. 

Several models have been proposed on how this might work, either by using activity templates to be reproduced (Miall and Wolpert, 1996) or error signals to be minimized (Kawato and Gomi, 1992;Montgomery et al., 2002). In the nervous system, these teaching signals might be provided by sensory feedback or other supervisory neural structures (Carey et al., 2005). One of these models that is primarily suitable for single-layer networks is called supervised Hebbian learning (SHL). documents.title: Predictive Coding Approximates Backprop Along Arbitrary Computation Graphs
documents.snippet:
A number of recent works have tried to provide biologically plausible approximations to backprop. The requirement of symmetry between the forwards and backwards weights has been questioned by Lillicrap, Cownden, Tweed, and Akerman (2016) who show that random fixed feedback weights suffice for effective learning. Recent additional work has shown that learning the backwards weights also helps (Akrout, Wilson, Humphreys, Lillicrap, & Tweed, 2019;Amit, 2019). 

A number of schemes have also been proposed to approximate backprop in a more biologically plausible manner, typically with local learning rules and/or Hebbian connectivity. These include target-prop (Lee, Zhang, Fischer, & Bengio, 2015) which approximate the backward gradients with trained inverse functions, but which fails to asymptotically compute the exact backprop gradients, and contrastive Hebbian (Scellier & Bengio, 2017;Scellier, Goyal, Binas, Mesnard, & Bengio, 2018;Seung, 2003) approaches which do exactly approximate backprop, but which require two separate learning phases and the storing of information across successive phases. There are also dendritic error theories (Guerguiev et al., 2017;Sacramento et al., 2018) which are computationally equivalent to predictive coding (Lillicrap, Santoro, Marris, Akerman, & Hinton, 2020;Whittington & Bogacz, 2019). Whittington and Bogacz (2017) showed that predictive coding can approximate backprop in MLP models, and demonstrated comparable performance on MNIST. We advance upon this work by extending the proof to arbitrary computation graphs, enabling the design of predictive coding variants of a range of standard machine learning architectures, which we show perform comparably to backprop on considerably more difficult tasks than MNIST. Our algorithm evinces asymptotic (and in practice rapid) convergence to the exact backprop gradients, does not require separate learning phases, and utilises only local information and largely Hebbian plasticity.
