attempts.answer:
Overview: a timescale mismatch that plasticity must bridge
- Neurons compute in milliseconds, but behavioral learning often occurs over seconds to minutes, while the durable changes underpinning learning are typically expressed over minutes to hours. Bridging this gap requires mechanisms that produce measurable changes in synaptic efficacy rapidly while organizing slower, persistent modifications in synaptic strength. <cite id="217260fb-0">There is a substantial gap between the timescales of neural electrical dynamics (1–100 ms) and organism behaviour during learning (seconds–minutes), motivating mechanisms that map fast dynamics to slower learning updates</cite>. <cite id="217260fb-2">Short-term changes induced by rapid spike sequences decay within a few hundred milliseconds (short-term plasticity), whereas long-term plasticity (LTP/LTD) can be induced within seconds but consolidated over hours, highlighting distinct fast and slow phases</cite>.

Mechanism 1: Short-term synaptic plasticity (STP/STD) as a fast gain-control and learning proxy
- Synapses rapidly modulate their efficacy via presynaptic mechanisms that change release probability and pool size of releasable vesicles, yielding facilitation (increased efficacy on a second-scale) or depression (decreased efficacy), over tens of milliseconds to minutes. <cite id="d84bc671-0">Short-term plasticity denotes modulation lasting tens of milliseconds to a few minutes, arising from presynaptic changes in release probability and release site availability; facilitation increases and depression decreases postsynaptic response to closely spaced spikes</cite>. <cite id="d84bc671-1">Short-term facilitation and depression occur on a timescale of milliseconds to seconds and are primarily governed by presynaptic vesicle depletion and calcium accumulation, with postsynaptic receptor desensitization contributing</cite>. <cite id="d84bc671-2">Short-term synaptic plasticity during and after repetitive presynaptic action potentials occurs on a timescale of milliseconds to minutes via changes in release probability and the readily releasable pool size</cite>.
- These rapid changes alter effective synaptic gain and input–output relationships within a spike train, enabling immediate adjustments to downstream firing without modifying long-term strengths. <cite id="d84bc671-0">Facilitation enhances information coding and transmission by promoting neurotransmitter release, providing a theoretical basis for fast, transient information transfer</cite>. <cite id="217260fb-2">Rapid decay of short-term changes suggests they are not for long-term memory but likely serve gain control, which is consistent with their use to modulate ongoing processing</cite>.

Mechanism 2: Spike timing, NMDA activation, and calcium transients that gate plasticity within seconds
- Plasticity is gated by the precise timing of pre- and postsynaptic spikes and the calcium transients that mediate it. <cite id="3464b92b-0">The peak of calcium transients underlying NMDA currents depends on spike timing: for pre-before-post (∆t>0) the peak decays on the NMDA receptor time constant τN and for post-before-pre (∆t<0) on a biphasic backpropagating action potential-associated calcium transient (τB), shaping LTP and LTD windows with widths set by these time constants</cite>. <cite id="3464b92b-0">Increasing spike train frequency ν increases calcium build-up for given timing, but at higher ν the dependence on ∆t decreases, explaining frequency-dependent STDP induction</cite>.
- Postsynaptic integration and NMDA access are constrained by rapidly deactivating AMPA receptors and magnesium block dynamics, yielding tens-of-millisecond integration windows for spike timing. <cite id="3464b92b-2">Postsynaptic potentials are effectively integrated within 20–30 ms because AMPA deactivation can be <1 ms and NMDA Mg2+ unblock is brief; disynaptic inhibition can further limit somatic integration to a few milliseconds</cite>.
- Presynaptic release dynamics and postsynaptic receptor kinetics together create a second-scale “credit assignment” that can be reshaped by network state and neuromodulators. <cite id="d84bc671-1">The initial probability of release biases whether a synapse tends toward depression or facilitation, and calcium accumulation and vesicle depletion in the presynaptic terminal govern facilitation/depression; postsynaptic desensitization contributes as well</cite>.

Mechanism 3: Dendritic and intrinsic nonlinearities that accelerate learning signals
- Backpropagating action potentials (bAPs) can coincide with excitatory inputs to trigger dendritic calcium spikes, producing highly nonlinear, amplifying responses that gate plasticity on a second-scale. <cite id="3464b92b-2">Backpropagating action potentials coinciding with EPSPs at the synapse may trigger dendritic calcium spikes, yielding highly nonlinear responses and shaping how inputs cooperatively drive plasticity</cite>.
- Spike threshold and membrane time constant introduce additional nonlinearity: neurons become more sensitive to synchronous inputs and less sensitive to unspecific background on short timescales, focusing synaptic changes onto temporally coherent signals. <cite id="3464b92b-2">Spike threshold is inversely related to preceding depolarization rate and spike rise time, endowing enhanced sensitivity to synchronous inputs; with higher input rates, somatic potentials compress and the temporal integration window shortens, demanding higher presynaptic precision</cite>.
- These intrinsic and dendritic mechanisms effectively compress information into brief, strong signatures that can trigger or suppress plasticity within seconds, even as the underlying synaptic machinery evolves over a broader range of timescales. <cite id="3464b92b-2">Backpropagating spikes and NMDA-dependent integration imply sub-100 ms windows where timing and synchrony are critical for plasticity induction, with dendritic nonlinearities sharpening these signatures</cite>.

Mechanism 4: Neuromodulation and network-state biasing of induction and early-phase consolidation
- Neuromodulators such as dopamine, acetylcholine, noradrenaline, and serotonin gate plasticity by reshaping learning windows and synaptic transmission, biasing induction toward behaviorally relevant synapses. <cite id="0ed1d9b4-1">Neuromodulators orchestrate neuronal activity across network and synaptic scales and control plasticity induction through metabotropic receptors, often by steering glutamatergic transmission to gate induction and maintenance</cite>. <cite id="0ed1d9b4-2">Neuromodulators can act by reshaping the STDP learning window (e.g., via a modulation parameter η) or by regulating synaptic transmission; dopamine via D2 receptors in the lateral amygdala and noradrenergic/cholinergic modulation in visual cortex exemplify these mechanisms</cite>.
- At the systems level, dopaminergic and cholinergic signals provide fast, widespread modulatory “gain” that can accelerate or suppress plasticity within seconds to minutes, aligning weight updates with salient events. <cite id="0ed1d9b4-0">Dopamine and other neurotransmitters modulate plasticity and memory, with neuromodulation often modeled as a global factor that scales plasticity and supports reward-based learning and active control of forgetting</cite>.
- Plasticity induction can begin within seconds, followed by slower consolidation over minutes to hours; early-phase LTP/LTD emerges within this window and anchors immediate behavioral improvements. <cite id="217260fb-2">The induction of long-term plasticity can be as fast as seconds, with additional consolidation after about an hour; early-phase LTP/LTD occurs before late-phase consolidation</cite>.

Computational and systems-level mechanisms that yield seconds-to-minutes learning
- Two-timescale rules: separate fast, error-suppressing adjustments from slow, learning-driven weight changes. <cite id="217260fb-1">Operating plasticity at a fast timescale to suppress immediate errors and a slow timescale to learn enables near-immediate task performance while long-term solutions consolidate later, outperforming online gradient learning in noisy conditions</cite>.
- Ensemble and population coding: across many synapses and neurons, correlated inputs and shared spikes can produce detectable, averaged plasticity changes within seconds as individual synaptic events integrate over time and space. <cite id="3464b92b-2">Synchrony, threshold nonlinearity, and compression of somatic responses mean only temporally precise inputs drive spikes; across populations, such precise, cooperative events accumulate to produce measurable synaptic changes over seconds</cite>.
- Network-level constraints and E/I balance: short-term plasticity in interneuron and principal cell synapses supports rapid gain control and stabilization, allowing immediate learning-like performance without destabilizing ongoing activity. <cite id="d84bc671-1">Short-term plasticity varies with initial release probability and is governed by presynaptic vesicle depletion and calcium accumulation, with postsynaptic desensitization contributing; it plays an important role in processing information and maintaining excitation-inhibition balance</cite>.

Putting it together: how “learning within seconds” emerges
- Rapid, second-scale synaptic and intrinsic dynamics provide the substrate for immediate changes in input gain and effective connectivity. Presynaptic facilitation and depression, AMPA/NMDA kinetics, and dendritic calcium spikes turn brief spike patterns into strong, localized calcium events that gate plasticity within tens of milliseconds to seconds. <cite id="d84bc671-0">Short-term facilitation and depression arise from vesicle pool and release probability dynamics, providing fast efficacy changes</cite>. <cite id="3464b92b-0">NMDA calcium peaks and STDP windows are set by spike timing and calcium decay time constants, explaining rapid induction dependence on precise timing and frequency</cite>. <cite id="3464b92b-2">AMPA deactivation and NMDA Mg-block dynamics constrain integration to 20–30 ms windows, while dendritic calcium spikes and spike threshold nonlinearities amplify synchronous inputs</cite>.
- Network state and neuromodulators bias these fast mechanisms toward behaviorally relevant inputs and accelerate induction. Dopamine, acetylcholine, noradrenaline, and serotonin reshape learning windows and glutamatergic transmission, effectively increasing the “neuromodulatory gain” on synaptic updates within seconds, while also setting up early biochemical cascades that mature into minutes-to-hour consolidation. <cite id="0ed1d9b4-1">Neuromodulators gate plasticity induction through metabotropic pathways and can steer glutamatergic transmission</cite>. <cite id="0ed1d9b4-2">Modulation of STDP timing windows by dopamine and cholinergic/noradrenergic pathways demonstrates rapid reshaping of learning rules</cite>. <cite id="217260fb-2">Induction can occur within seconds, with late-phase consolidation after ~an hour</cite>.
- At the systems level, neurons and circuits exploit two-timescale rules and population coding to display near-instant improvements in performance while committing only slowly to synaptic change. This explains why animals can show behavioral adaptation within seconds even though the molecular and structural changes in synapses take minutes to hours to consolidate. <cite id="217260fb-1">A multiscale plasticity rule with fast suppression of immediate errors and slow learning yields accurate near-immediate task performance before long-term weight changes consolidate</cite>. <cite id="217260fb-0">Nonlinear interactions between fast and slow plasticity mechanisms at synapses bridge the ms-to-seconds-to-minutes gap in learning</cite>.

Remaining gaps and outlook
- Quantitative mapping of how specific neuromodulators and network states shift each synaptic parameter (release probability, vesicle pool, AMPA/NMDA kinetics, calcium dynamics) across brain regions remains an active area; integrating single-synapse biophysics with circuit-level signals is key to predicting when second-scale learning will generalize to population-level behavior. <cite id="d84bc671-1">Short-term plasticity depends on initial release probability and presynaptic calcium/vesicle dynamics, but functional importance varies across synapse types and factors</cite>. <cite id="3464b92b-2">Integration windows and nonlinearities are shaped by receptor kinetics and inhibition; their precise tuning across circuits likely determines how rapidly learning manifests</cite>. <cite id="0ed1d9b4-1">Neuromodulators control plasticity outcomes by steering glutamatergic transmission, but pathway-specific mechanisms need systematic mapping</cite>.
- Bridging experiments that combine millisecond-resolved calcium imaging, presynaptic release measurements, neuromodulator perturbations, and closed-loop behavioral assays will help delineate the seconds-to-minutes plasticity “pipeline” and identify when fast changes reliably translate into durable learning. <cite id="217260fb-0">Future progress requires studies that map nonlinearities of fast and slow plasticity mechanisms and their joint interactions across synapses and networks</cite>.

In summary, biological neurons “learn within seconds” by coupling ultrafast synaptic and intrinsic nonlinear dynamics—with precise spike timing, rapid NMDA/AMPA transients, and dendritic calcium amplification—to fast network-state and neuromodulatory signals. These mechanisms reshape synaptic gain and effective connectivity on a second-scale, while biochemical pathways take over to consolidate changes over minutes to hours, yielding immediate behavioral improvements with a gradual imprinting of durable memory. <cite id="d84bc671-0">Short-term facilitation/depression provide millisecond–second efficacy changes by altering release probability and vesicle pool availability</cite> <cite id="3464b92b-0">and spike-timing-dependent calcium dynamics define sub-100 ms windows for LTP/LTD induction</cite> <cite id="3464b92b-2">through AMPA/NMDA kinetics and dendritic calcium spikes</cite> <cite id="217260fb-2">that can be rapidly biased by neuromodulators and network state, with durable changes consolidating over minutes to hours</cite>.

Snippet: Synaptic plasticity exists across different timescales. For instance, synaptic changes induced by a sequence of four presynaptic spikes in rapid sequence typically decay within a few hundred milliseconds [42][43][44] and are called short-term plasticity. The rapid decay implies that the changes are not useful for long-term memory formation, but more likely involved in gain control [42]. 

Other forms of plasticity induced by classic induction protocols [45 -47] can have long-term effects on the timescale of hours or more. Long-term plasticity is therefore potentially useful for memory formation [2]. We remind the reader that the induction of long-term plasticity can be as fast as seconds, but the induced changes persist for much longer. Depending on the direction of synaptic change, we speak of long-term potentiation (LTP) or long-term depression (LTD). 

Under suitable conditions the changes induced by a protocol of LTP or LTD are further consolidated after about an hour [48][49][50]. These effects are often referred to as latephase long-term plasticity. In the rest of the paper, we focus on plasticity induction and the early phase of longterm plasticity and neglect consolidation and maintenance. 

The diverse effects of long-term plasticity can be cast into a mathematical framework which describes the change of synaptic efficacy over time. Apart from a few notable exceptions [17,[51][52][53][54], the vast majority of models of long-term plasticity assume a one-dimensional synaptic state space which represents the synaptic efficacy or weight w ij of a  in which the function G, often called the 'learning rule', is a member of an infinite dimensional function space G, the space of all possible learning rules. This space is strongly constrained if we only focus on plausible learning rules, which are the rules in agreement with experimental findings.

Title: A mathematical model of synaptotagmin 7 revealing functional importance of short-term synaptic plasticity
Snippet: Synapses have been shown to undergo dynamical modulations in postsynaptic responses following stimulation by specific patterns of action potentials at the presynaptic terminal. Short-term plasticity is one of the main forms of plasticities displayed in central neurons (Citri and Malenka, 2007). Short-term synaptic plasticity denotes the modulation that lasts from tens of milliseconds to a few minutes. It originates from presynaptic mechanisms through modulating the presynaptic release probability and the site availability for release (Regehr, 2012). The plastic nature of synaptic transmission provides a theoretical basis for information transfer and memory formation (Martin et al., 2000;Klyachko and Stevens, 2006). 

Short-term facilitation and depression are typical forms of short-term synaptic plasticity in central synapses (Zucker and Regehr, 2002). In synapses displaying short-term facilitation, postsynaptic response by the second of two closely spaced presynaptic action potential (APs) is larger than that by the first one, and thus synapses show increased synaptic efficacy (Regehr, 2012). On the contrary, short-term depression refers to a lower postsynaptic response by the second of two closely spaced presynaptic APs compared to the postsynaptic response by the first one, and leads to a reduction in synaptic strength. Mostly, synaptic strength results from a combination of short-term facilitation and depression, depending on the timing of presynaptic stimulation (Zucker and Regehr, 2002). However, the functional importance of short-term plasticity in the synapse is not well understood. 

Facilitation can enhance the information coding and transmission across a synapse by promoting the neurotransmitter release by presynaptic stimulation (Abbott and Regehr, 2004). The mechanism underlying the facilitation in Schaffer collaterals (SCs) remains a mystery and is different from the Ca 2+ buffer saturation mechanism, which accounts for the facilitation in several critical brain areas (Blatow et al., 2003;Jackman et al., 2016).
</snippet>

Title: The short-term plasticity of VIP interneurons in motor cortex
Snippet: Information in the brain is transmitted through synaptic connections between neurons in a dynamic manner. This allows for the activity-dependent modification of synaptic strength between neurons, a concept known as synaptic plasticity. Long lasting changes in synaptic strength are widely believed to underlie learning and information storage in the brain (Bliss and Collingridge, 1993;Malenka and Bear, 2004;Nabavi et al., 2014). But there exist other forms of plasticity, such as short-term facilitation and short-term depression, that occur on a much faster time scale on the order of milliseconds to seconds. 

Short-term plasticity is an important feature for processing information and maintaining the balance of excitation and inhibition (E/I) in the brain (Blackman et al., 2013). The initial probability McFarlan et al. 10.3389/fnsyn.2024.1433977 Frontiers in Synaptic Neuroscience 02 frontiersin.org of release dictates the outcome of short-term plasticity at a given synapse. 

A synapse with a high initial probability of release, for example, will tend to exhibit short-term depression whereas a synapse with a low initial probability of release will tend to exhibit short-term facilitation. Mechanistically, short-term plasticity is primarily governed by changes in the presynaptic terminal, such as synaptic vesicle depletion and the accumulation of calcium in presynaptic terminals (Regehr, 2012). However, postsynaptic factors such as receptor desensitization also contribute to synaptic short-term dynamics (Rozov and Burnashev, 1999;Rozov et al., 2001). Short-term plasticity varies with a number of different factors.
</snippet>

Title: Analysis of the intraspinal calcium dynamics and its implications for the plasticity of spiking neurons.
Snippet: Calcium transients due to NMDA currents are believed to play a major role in many forms of synaptic plasticity. We have recently shown that a model based on these transients can account for various different plasticityinduction protocols [28]. In this paper, we compute analytically the calcium dynamics evoked by pairs of pre-and postsynaptic spikes under different conditions, so that the variables that control calcium transients and impact synaptic plasticity can be investigated. 

We showed that the peak of the calcium transients depends on the ∆t: for ∆t > 0, the peak concentration decays with the time constant τ N of the NMDAR, and for ∆t < 0, it decays with the time constant τ B of the BPAP. Therefore, if spike time dependent plasticity, in-deed depends on the calcium transients, τ N and τ B will determine the width of the pre-post LTP and the post-pre LTD windows, respectively. These results were confirmed by simulations, in which the approximations we used in the calculations were relaxed. The ∆t dependence of the peak calcium transient is similar in the more complex and realistic case where the BPAP dynamics is composed of a fast and a slow component: the difference lies in the ∆t < 0 case, which now depends on the combination of the two time constants. The two-component BPAP allows a sharper transition between the post-before-pre and the pre-before-post STDP window, which is further enhanced by a fast calcium dynamics. We also showed that, besides the timing of the pre and post-spikes, the peak values of the calcium transients also depend on the frequency ν of the pre and postsynaptic conditioning, increasing for greater values of ν. However, at higher frequencies, the dependence on ∆t decreases. The amount of calcium build-up at a given frequency depends on the system parameters; slower time constants results in more temporal integration. Temporal integration of calcium transients, as described here, can explain why, in some cases, the induction of STDP is frequency-dependent. 

One of the predictions of the unified calcium model is that there exists a pre-before-post LTD for values of ∆t greater than the ones that elicit LTP [28].
</snippet>

Title: Neural synchrony in cortical networks: mechanisms and implications for neural information processing and coding
Snippet: The temporal precision of neuronal communication crucially depends on a number of basic cellular properties. Spike-timing-dependent plasticity rules for modifications in synaptic strength indicate that postsynaptic potentials are effectively integrated within only 20-30 ms (Dan and Poo, 2006;Caporale and Dan, 2008). Such short integration times mainly result from rapidly deactivating AMPA receptors that can have deactivation time constants of less than a millisecond (Hestrin, 1993;Geiger et al., 1997;Magee, 2000) and indirectly control the kinetics of NMDA receptor currents by only allowing for a correspondingly short release of the magnesium block (Oertner, 2009;Holbro et al., 2010). In addition, disynaptic feedforward inhibition may confine the effective integration time window in the soma to a few millisecond (Pouille and Scanziani, 2001). Backpropagating action potentials coinciding at the synapse with excitatory postsynaptic potentials may trigger dendritic calcium spikes and in this way cause highly nonlinear responses (Stuart et al., 1997;Schiller et al., 1998;Larkum et al., 1999;Stuart and Häusser, 2001;London and Häusser, 2005). Another nonlinear element is the spike threshold which is inversely related to the rate of membrane depolarization preceding a spike and the rise time of the action potential, endowing neurons with enhanced sensitivity to synchronous inputs (Azouz and Gray, 2000;Harnett et al., 2012;Fontaine et al., 2014). With increasing input rates, both the amplitude and duration of somatic potentials in response to synaptic input are reduced, resulting in a shortening of the temporal integration window and requiring a yet higher precision of presynaptic signals to drive the neuron to fire (Azouz and Gray, 2003;Léger et al., 2005).

Title: Neuromodulators and Long-Term Synaptic Plasticity in Learning and Memory: A Steered-Glutamatergic Perspective
Snippet: The molecular pathways underlying the induction and maintenance of long-term synaptic plasticity have been extensively investigated revealing various mechanisms by which neurons control their synaptic strength. The dynamic nature of neuronal connections combined with plasticity-mediated long-lasting structural and functional alterations provide valuable insights into neuronal encoding processes as molecular substrates of not only learning and memory but potentially other sensory, motor and behavioural functions that reflect previous experience. However, one key element receiving little attention in the study of synaptic plasticity is the role of neuromodulators, which are known to orchestrate neuronal activity on brain-wide, network and synaptic scales. We aim to review current evidence on the mechanisms by which certain modulators, namely dopamine, acetylcholine, noradrenaline and serotonin, control synaptic plasticity induction through corresponding metabotropic receptors in a pathway-specific manner. Lastly, we propose that neuromodulators control plasticity outcomes through steering glutamatergic transmission, thereby gating its induction and maintenance.
</snippet>

Overview: a timescale mismatch that plasticity must bridge
- Neurons compute in milliseconds, but behavioral learning often occurs over seconds to minutes, while the durable changes underpinning learning are typically expressed over minutes to hours. Bridging this gap requires mechanisms that produce measurable changes in synaptic efficacy rapidly while organizing slower, persistent modifications in synaptic strength. <cite id="217260fb-0">There is a substantial gap between the timescales of neural electrical dynamics (1–100 ms) and organism behaviour during learning (seconds–minutes), motivating mechanisms that map fast dynamics to slower learning updates</cite>. <cite id="217260fb-2">Short-term changes induced by rapid spike sequences decay within a few hundred milliseconds (short-term plasticity), whereas long-term plasticity (LTP/LTD) can be induced within seconds but consolidated over hours, highlighting distinct fast and slow phases</cite>.

Mechanism 1: Short-term synaptic plasticity (STP/STD) as a fast gain-control and learning proxy
- Synapses rapidly modulate their efficacy via presynaptic mechanisms that change release probability and pool size of releasable vesicles, yielding facilitation (increased efficacy on a second-scale) or depression (decreased efficacy), over tens of milliseconds to minutes. <cite id="d84bc671-0">Short-term plasticity denotes modulation lasting tens of milliseconds to a few minutes, arising from presynaptic changes in release probability and release site availability; facilitation increases and depression decreases postsynaptic response to closely spaced spikes</cite>. <cite id="d84bc671-1">Short-term facilitation and depression occur on a timescale of milliseconds to seconds and are primarily governed by presynaptic vesicle depletion and calcium accumulation, with postsynaptic receptor desensitization contributing</cite>. <cite id="d84bc671-2">Short-term synaptic plasticity during and after repetitive presynaptic action potentials occurs on a timescale of milliseconds to minutes via changes in release probability and the readily releasable pool size</cite>.
- These rapid changes alter effective synaptic gain and input–output relationships within a spike train, enabling immediate adjustments to downstream firing without modifying long-term strengths. <cite id="d84bc671-0">Facilitation enhances information coding and transmission by promoting neurotransmitter release, providing a theoretical basis for fast, transient information transfer</cite>. <cite id="217260fb-2">Rapid decay of short-term changes suggests they are not for long-term memory but likely serve gain control, which is consistent with their use to modulate ongoing processing</cite>.

Mechanism 2: Spike timing, NMDA activation, and calcium transients that gate plasticity within seconds
- Plasticity is gated by the precise timing of pre- and postsynaptic spikes and the calcium transients that mediate it. <cite id="3464b92b-0">The peak of calcium transients underlying NMDA currents depends on spike timing: for pre-before-post (∆t>0) the peak decays on the NMDA receptor time constant τN and for post-before-pre (∆t<0) on a biphasic backpropagating action potential-associated calcium transient (τB), shaping LTP and LTD windows with widths set by these time constants</cite>. <cite id="3464b92b-0">Increasing spike train frequency ν increases calcium build-up for given timing, but at higher ν the dependence on ∆t decreases, explaining frequency-dependent STDP induction</cite>.
- Postsynaptic integration and NMDA access are constrained by rapidly deactivating AMPA receptors and magnesium block dynamics, yielding tens-of-millisecond integration windows for spike timing. <cite id="3464b92b-2">Postsynaptic potentials are effectively integrated within 20–30 ms because AMPA deactivation can be <1 ms and NMDA Mg2+ unblock is brief; disynaptic inhibition can further limit somatic integration to a few milliseconds</cite>.
- Presynaptic release dynamics and postsynaptic receptor kinetics together create a second-scale “credit assignment” that can be reshaped by network state and neuromodulators. <cite id="d84bc671-1">The initial probability of release biases whether a synapse tends toward depression or facilitation, and calcium accumulation and vesicle depletion in the presynaptic terminal govern facilitation/depression; postsynaptic desensitization contributes as well</cite>.

Mechanism 3: Dendritic and intrinsic nonlinearities that accelerate learning signals
- Backpropagating action potentials (bAPs) can coincide with excitatory inputs to trigger dendritic calcium spikes, producing highly nonlinear, amplifying responses that gate plasticity on a second-scale. <cite id="3464b92b-2">Backpropagating action potentials coinciding with EPSPs at the synapse may trigger dendritic calcium spikes, yielding highly nonlinear responses and shaping how inputs cooperatively drive plasticity</cite>.
- Spike threshold and membrane time constant introduce additional nonlinearity: neurons become more sensitive to synchronous inputs and less sensitive to unspecific background on short timescales, focusing synaptic changes onto temporally coherent signals. <cite id="3464b92b-2">Spike threshold is inversely related to preceding depolarization rate and spike rise time, endowing enhanced sensitivity to synchronous inputs; with higher input rates, somatic potentials compress and the temporal integration window shortens, demanding higher presynaptic precision</cite>.
- These intrinsic and dendritic mechanisms effectively compress information into brief, strong signatures that can trigger or suppress plasticity within seconds, even as the underlying synaptic machinery evolves over a broader range of timescales. <cite id="3464b92b-2">Backpropagating spikes and NMDA-dependent integration imply sub-100 ms windows where timing and synchrony are critical for plasticity induction, with dendritic nonlinearities sharpening these signatures</cite>.

Mechanism 4: Neuromodulation and network-state biasing of induction and early-phase consolidation
- Neuromodulators such as dopamine, acetylcholine, noradrenaline, and serotonin gate plasticity by reshaping learning windows and synaptic transmission, biasing induction toward behaviorally relevant synapses. <cite id="0ed1d9b4-1">Neuromodulators orchestrate neuronal activity across network and synaptic scales and control plasticity induction through metabotropic receptors, often by steering glutamatergic transmission to gate induction and maintenance</cite>. <cite id="0ed1d9b4-2">Neuromodulators can act by reshaping the STDP learning window (e.g., via a modulation parameter η) or by regulating synaptic transmission; dopamine via D2 receptors in the lateral amygdala and noradrenergic/cholinergic modulation in visual cortex exemplify these mechanisms</cite>.
- At the systems level, dopaminergic and cholinergic signals provide fast, widespread modulatory “gain” that can accelerate or suppress plasticity within seconds to minutes, aligning weight updates with salient events. <cite id="0ed1d9b4-0">Dopamine and other neurotransmitters modulate plasticity and memory, with neuromodulation often modeled as a global factor that scales plasticity and supports reward-based learning and active control of forgetting</cite>.
- Plasticity induction can begin within seconds, followed by slower consolidation over minutes to hours; early-phase LTP/LTD emerges within this window and anchors immediate behavioral improvements. <cite id="217260fb-2">The induction of long-term plasticity can be as fast as seconds, with additional consolidation after about an hour; early-phase LTP/LTD occurs before late-phase consolidation</cite>.

Computational and systems-level mechanisms that yield seconds-to-minutes learning
- Two-timescale rules: separate fast, error-suppressing adjustments from slow, learning-driven weight changes. <cite id="217260fb-1">Operating plasticity at a fast timescale to suppress immediate errors and a slow timescale to learn enables near-immediate task performance while long-term solutions consolidate later, outperforming online gradient learning in noisy conditions</cite>.
- Ensemble and population coding: across many synapses and neurons, correlated inputs and shared spikes can produce detectable, averaged plasticity changes within seconds as individual synaptic events integrate over time and space. <cite id="3464b92b-2">Synchrony, threshold nonlinearity, and compression of somatic responses mean only temporally precise inputs drive spikes; across populations, such precise, cooperative events accumulate to produce measurable synaptic changes over seconds</cite>.
- Network-level constraints and E/I balance: short-term plasticity in interneuron and principal cell synapses supports rapid gain control and stabilization, allowing immediate learning-like performance without destabilizing ongoing activity. <cite id="d84bc671-1">Short-term plasticity varies with initial release probability and is governed by presynaptic vesicle depletion and calcium accumulation, with postsynaptic desensitization contributing; it plays an important role in processing information and maintaining excitation-inhibition balance</cite>.

Putting it together: how “learning within seconds” emerges
- Rapid, second-scale synaptic and intrinsic dynamics provide the substrate for immediate changes in input gain and effective connectivity. Presynaptic facilitation and depression, AMPA/NMDA kinetics, and dendritic calcium spikes turn brief spike patterns into strong, localized calcium events that gate plasticity within tens of milliseconds to seconds. <cite id="d84bc671-0">Short-term facilitation and depression arise from vesicle pool and release probability dynamics, providing fast efficacy changes</cite>. <cite id="3464b92b-0">NMDA calcium peaks and STDP windows are set by spike timing and calcium decay time constants, explaining rapid induction dependence on precise timing and frequency</cite>. <cite id="3464b92b-2">AMPA deactivation and NMDA Mg-block dynamics constrain integration to 20–30 ms windows, while dendritic calcium spikes and spike threshold nonlinearities amplify synchronous inputs</cite>.
- Network state and neuromodulators bias these fast mechanisms toward behaviorally relevant inputs and accelerate induction. Dopamine, acetylcholine, noradrenaline, and serotonin reshape learning windows and glutamatergic transmission, effectively increasing the “neuromodulatory gain” on synaptic updates within seconds, while also setting up early biochemical cascades that mature into minutes-to-hour consolidation. <cite id="0ed1d9b4-1">Neuromodulators gate plasticity induction through metabotropic pathways and can steer glutamatergic transmission</cite>. <cite id="0ed1d9b4-2">Modulation of STDP timing windows by dopamine and cholinergic/noradrenergic pathways demonstrates rapid reshaping of learning rules</cite>. <cite id="217260fb-2">Induction can occur within seconds, with late-phase consolidation after ~an hour</cite>.
- At the systems level, neurons and circuits exploit two-timescale rules and population coding to display near-instant improvements in performance while committing only slowly to synaptic change. This explains why animals can show behavioral adaptation within seconds even though the molecular and structural changes in synapses take minutes to hours to consolidate. <cite id="217260fb-1">A multiscale plasticity rule with fast suppression of immediate errors and slow learning yields accurate near-immediate task performance before long-term weight changes consolidate</cite>. <cite id="217260fb-0">Nonlinear interactions between fast and slow plasticity mechanisms at synapses bridge the ms-to-seconds-to-minutes gap in learning</cite>.

Remaining gaps and outlook
- Quantitative mapping of how specific neuromodulators and network states shift each synaptic parameter (release probability, vesicle pool, AMPA/NMDA kinetics, calcium dynamics) across brain regions remains an active area; integrating single-synapse biophysics with circuit-level signals is key to predicting when second-scale learning will generalize to population-level behavior. <cite id="d84bc671-1">Short-term plasticity depends on initial release probability and presynaptic calcium/vesicle dynamics, but functional importance varies across synapse types and factors</cite>. <cite id="3464b92b-2">Integration windows and nonlinearities are shaped by receptor kinetics and inhibition; their precise tuning across circuits likely determines how rapidly learning manifests</cite>. <cite id="0ed1d9b4-1">Neuromodulators control plasticity outcomes by steering glutamatergic transmission, but pathway-specific mechanisms need systematic mapping</cite>.
- Bridging experiments that combine millisecond-resolved calcium imaging, presynaptic release measurements, neuromodulator perturbations, and closed-loop behavioral assays will help delineate the seconds-to-minutes plasticity “pipeline” and identify when fast changes reliably translate into durable learning. <cite id="217260fb-0">Future progress requires studies that map nonlinearities of fast and slow plasticity mechanisms and their joint interactions across synapses and networks</cite>.

In summary, biological neurons “learn within seconds” by coupling ultrafast synaptic and intrinsic nonlinear dynamics—with precise spike timing, rapid NMDA/AMPA transients, and dendritic calcium amplification—to fast network-state and neuromodulatory signals. These mechanisms reshape synaptic gain and effective connectivity on a second-scale, while biochemical pathways take over to consolidate changes over minutes to hours, yielding immediate behavioral improvements with a gradual imprinting of durable memory. <cite id="d84bc671-0">Short-term facilitation/depression provide millisecond–second efficacy changes by altering release probability and vesicle pool availability</cite> <cite id="3464b92b-0">and spike-timing-dependent calcium dynamics define sub-100 ms windows for LTP/LTD induction</cite> <cite id="3464b92b-2">through AMPA/NMDA kinetics and dendritic calcium spikes</cite> <cite id="217260fb-2">that can be rapidly biased by neuromodulators and network state, with durable changes consolidating over minutes to hours</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Nonlinear slow-timescale mechanisms in synaptic plasticity.
Snippet: Learning and memory rely on synapses changing their strengths in response to neural activity. However, there is a substantial gap between the timescales of neural electrical dynamics (1-100 ms) and organism behaviour during learning (seconds-minutes). What mechanisms bridge this timescale gap? What are the implications for theories of brain learning? Here I first cover experimental evidence for slow-timescale factors in plasticity induction. Then I review possible underlying cellular and synaptic mechanisms, and insights from recent computational models that incorporate such slow-timescale variables. I conclude that future progress in understanding brain learning across timescales will require both experimental and computational modelling studies that map out the nonlinearities implemented by both fast and slow plasticity mechanisms at synapses, and crucially, their joint interactions.

For instance, synaptic changes induced by a sequence of four presynaptic spikes in rapid sequence typically decay within a few hundred milliseconds [42][43][44] and are called short-term plasticity. The rapid decay implies that the changes are not useful for long-term memory formation, but more likely involved in gain control [42]. 

Other forms of plasticity induced by classic induction protocols [45 -47] can have long-term effects on the timescale of hours or more. Long-term plasticity is therefore potentially useful for memory formation [2]. We remind the reader that the induction of long-term plasticity can be as fast as seconds, but the induced changes persist for much longer. Depending on the direction of synaptic change, we speak of long-term potentiation (LTP) or long-term depression (LTD). 

Under suitable conditions the changes induced by a protocol of LTP or LTD are further consolidated after about an hour [48][49][50]. These effects are often referred to as latephase long-term plasticity. In the rest of the paper, we focus on plasticity induction and the early phase of longterm plasticity and neglect consolidation and maintenance. 

The diverse effects of long-term plasticity can be cast into a mathematical framework which describes the change of synaptic efficacy over time. Apart from a few notable exceptions [17,[51][52][53][54], the vast majority of models of long-term plasticity assume a one-dimensional synaptic state space which represents the synaptic efficacy or weight w ij of a  in which the function G, often called the 'learning rule', is a member of an infinite dimensional function space G, the space of all possible learning rules. This space is strongly constrained if we only focus on plausible learning rules, which are the rules in agreement with experimental findings.

snippet.text: Learning and memory rely on synapses changing their strengths in response to neural activity. However, there is a substantial gap between the timescales of neural electrical dynamics (1-100 ms) and organism behaviour during learning (seconds-minutes). What mechanisms bridge this timescale gap? What are the implications for theories of brain learning? Here I first cover experimental evidence for slow-timescale factors in plasticity induction. Then I review possible underlying cellular and synaptic mechanisms, and insights from recent computational models that incorporate such slow-timescale variables. I conclude that future progress in understanding brain learning across timescales will require both experimental and computational modelling studies that map out the nonlinearities implemented by both fast and slow plasticity mechanisms at synapses, and crucially, their joint interactions.

snippet.text: We proposed that synaptic plasticity should operate at two timescales: a fast timescale to suppress immediate errors, and a slow timescale to learn. This multiscale plasticity rule significantly outperforms online gradient-based learning, confers robustness to noise and other perturbations, and means that neurons can accurately perform a task almost immediately -well before learning has stored a longer-term solution in the weights.

Title: A mathematical model of synaptotagmin 7 revealing functional importance of short-term synaptic plasticity
Snippet: Synapses have been shown to undergo dynamical modulations in postsynaptic responses following stimulation by specific patterns of action potentials at the presynaptic terminal. Short-term plasticity is one of the main forms of plasticities displayed in central neurons (Citri and Malenka, 2007). Short-term synaptic plasticity denotes the modulation that lasts from tens of milliseconds to a few minutes. It originates from presynaptic mechanisms through modulating the presynaptic release probability and the site availability for release (Regehr, 2012). The plastic nature of synaptic transmission provides a theoretical basis for information transfer and memory formation (Martin et al., 2000;Klyachko and Stevens, 2006). 

Short-term facilitation and depression are typical forms of short-term synaptic plasticity in central synapses (Zucker and Regehr, 2002). In synapses displaying short-term facilitation, postsynaptic response by the second of two closely spaced presynaptic action potential (APs) is larger than that by the first one, and thus synapses show increased synaptic efficacy (Regehr, 2012). On the contrary, short-term depression refers to a lower postsynaptic response by the second of two closely spaced presynaptic APs compared to the postsynaptic response by the first one, and leads to a reduction in synaptic strength. Mostly, synaptic strength results from a combination of short-term facilitation and depression, depending on the timing of presynaptic stimulation (Zucker and Regehr, 2002). However, the functional importance of short-term plasticity in the synapse is not well understood. 

Facilitation can enhance the information coding and transmission across a synapse by promoting the neurotransmitter release by presynaptic stimulation (Abbott and Regehr, 2004). The mechanism underlying the facilitation in Schaffer collaterals (SCs) remains a mystery and is different from the Ca 2+ buffer saturation mechanism, which accounts for the facilitation in several critical brain areas (Blatow et al., 2003;Jackman et al., 2016).

Title: The short-term plasticity of VIP interneurons in motor cortex
Snippet: Information in the brain is transmitted through synaptic connections between neurons in a dynamic manner. This allows for the activity-dependent modification of synaptic strength between neurons, a concept known as synaptic plasticity. Long lasting changes in synaptic strength are widely believed to underlie learning and information storage in the brain (Bliss and Collingridge, 1993;Malenka and Bear, 2004;Nabavi et al., 2014). But there exist other forms of plasticity, such as short-term facilitation and short-term depression, that occur on a much faster time scale on the order of milliseconds to seconds. 

Short-term plasticity is an important feature for processing information and maintaining the balance of excitation and inhibition (E/I) in the brain (Blackman et al., 2013). The initial probability McFarlan et al. 10.3389/fnsyn.2024.1433977 Frontiers in Synaptic Neuroscience 02 frontiersin.org of release dictates the outcome of short-term plasticity at a given synapse. 

A synapse with a high initial probability of release, for example, will tend to exhibit short-term depression whereas a synapse with a low initial probability of release will tend to exhibit short-term facilitation. Mechanistically, short-term plasticity is primarily governed by changes in the presynaptic terminal, such as synaptic vesicle depletion and the accumulation of calcium in presynaptic terminals (Regehr, 2012). However, postsynaptic factors such as receptor desensitization also contribute to synaptic short-term dynamics (Rozov and Burnashev, 1999;Rozov et al., 2001). Short-term plasticity varies with a number of different factors.

Title: Analysis of the intraspinal calcium dynamics and its implications for the plasticity of spiking neurons.
Snippet: Calcium transients due to NMDA currents are believed to play a major role in many forms of synaptic plasticity. We have recently shown that a model based on these transients can account for various different plasticityinduction protocols [28]. In this paper, we compute analytically the calcium dynamics evoked by pairs of pre-and postsynaptic spikes under different conditions, so that the variables that control calcium transients and impact synaptic plasticity can be investigated. 

We showed that the peak of the calcium transients depends on the ∆t: for ∆t > 0, the peak concentration decays with the time constant τ N of the NMDAR, and for ∆t < 0, it decays with the time constant τ B of the BPAP. Therefore, if spike time dependent plasticity, in-deed depends on the calcium transients, τ N and τ B will determine the width of the pre-post LTP and the post-pre LTD windows, respectively. These results were confirmed by simulations, in which the approximations we used in the calculations were relaxed. The ∆t dependence of the peak calcium transient is similar in the more complex and realistic case where the BPAP dynamics is composed of a fast and a slow component: the difference lies in the ∆t < 0 case, which now depends on the combination of the two time constants. The two-component BPAP allows a sharper transition between the post-before-pre and the pre-before-post STDP window, which is further enhanced by a fast calcium dynamics. We also showed that, besides the timing of the pre and post-spikes, the peak values of the calcium transients also depend on the frequency ν of the pre and postsynaptic conditioning, increasing for greater values of ν. However, at higher frequencies, the dependence on ∆t decreases. The amount of calcium build-up at a given frequency depends on the system parameters; slower time constants results in more temporal integration. Temporal integration of calcium transients, as described here, can explain why, in some cases, the induction of STDP is frequency-dependent. 

One of the predictions of the unified calcium model is that there exists a pre-before-post LTD for values of ∆t greater than the ones that elicit LTP [28].

Title: Neural synchrony in cortical networks: mechanisms and implications for neural information processing and coding
Snippet: The temporal precision of neuronal communication crucially depends on a number of basic cellular properties. Spike-timing-dependent plasticity rules for modifications in synaptic strength indicate that postsynaptic potentials are effectively integrated within only 20-30 ms (Dan and Poo, 2006;Caporale and Dan, 2008). Such short integration times mainly result from rapidly deactivating AMPA receptors that can have deactivation time constants of less than a millisecond (Hestrin, 1993;Geiger et al., 1997;Magee, 2000) and indirectly control the kinetics of NMDA receptor currents by only allowing for a correspondingly short release of the magnesium block (Oertner, 2009;Holbro et al., 2010). In addition, disynaptic feedforward inhibition may confine the effective integration time window in the soma to a few millisecond (Pouille and Scanziani, 2001). Backpropagating action potentials coinciding at the synapse with excitatory postsynaptic potentials may trigger dendritic calcium spikes and in this way cause highly nonlinear responses (Stuart et al., 1997;Schiller et al., 1998;Larkum et al., 1999;Stuart and Häusser, 2001;London and Häusser, 2005). Another nonlinear element is the spike threshold which is inversely related to the rate of membrane depolarization preceding a spike and the rise time of the action potential, endowing neurons with enhanced sensitivity to synchronous inputs (Azouz and Gray, 2000;Harnett et al., 2012;Fontaine et al., 2014). With increasing input rates, both the amplitude and duration of somatic potentials in response to synaptic input are reduced, resulting in a shortening of the temporal integration window and requiring a yet higher precision of presynaptic signals to drive the neuron to fire (Azouz and Gray, 2003;Léger et al., 2005).

Backpropagating action potentials coinciding at the synapse with excitatory postsynaptic potentials may trigger dendritic calcium spikes and in this way cause highly nonlinear responses (Stuart et al., 1997;Schiller et al., 1998;Larkum et al., 1999;Stuart and Häusser, 2001;London and Häusser, 2005). Another nonlinear element is the spike threshold which is inversely related to the rate of membrane depolarization preceding a spike and the rise time of the action potential, endowing neurons with enhanced sensitivity to synchronous inputs (Azouz and Gray, 2000;Harnett et al., 2012;Fontaine et al., 2014). With increasing input rates, both the amplitude and duration of somatic potentials in response to synaptic input are reduced, resulting in a shortening of the temporal integration window and requiring a yet higher precision of presynaptic signals to drive the neuron to fire (Azouz and Gray, 2003;Léger et al., 2005).

attempts.answer:
# Summary

Hebbian plasticity implements credit assignment by adjusting synapses based on local correlations between presynaptic and postsynaptic activity, most concretely through spike-timing–dependent plasticity (STDP) that potentiates aligned spike pairs and depresses reverse-aligned ones. In biological networks, the sign and specificity of these updates are “error-corrected” by recurrent and feedback microcircuits that encode neuron-specific credit signals (e.g., top-down disinhibition or inhibitory gating), by local error proxies computed from activity differences (e.g., BCM-style threshold dynamics or predictive coding decompositions), and by the statistics of background noise that stabilize or steer correlations. These mechanisms allow Hebbian-like rules to approximate gradient-based credit assignment, stabilize runaway potentiation, and perform comparably to backpropagation on hierarchical tasks while remaining biologically and energetically plausible. <cite id="97c64844-0">How neuronal circuits achieve credit assignment remains a central unsolved question; models that assume distinct compartments for local error signals can be reconciled with phenomenological Hebbian rules when recurrent inhibition explicitly influences plasticity, yielding error-modulated learning</cite><cite id="97c64844-2">a Hebbian rule with explicit inhibition dependence can decode credit signals from a dis-inhibitory microcircuit, stabilize runaway Hebbian plasticity, resemble phenomenological rules, and perform comparably to backpropagation on vision benchmarks</cite><cite id="97c64844-3">predictive coding with local Hebbian plasticity decomposes error into target- and predicted-value terms, yielding robust single Hebbian updates that avoid mistaken weight changes when targets are absent</cite><cite id="70553646-0">spike-based encoding with Hebbian/STDP is robust to noise, and background synaptic activity can promote discrimination and even relax stability constraints through random external noise</cite><cite id="4698068d-3">correlation-based Hebbian rules for spiking neurons tend to stabilize correlations between inputs and outputs, and BCM-style models have strong experimental support in visual cortex</cite>.

# From Correlation Rules to Credit Assignment: Why Sign and Locality Matter

Hebbian plasticity is defined by changes that depend on the temporal correlations of pre- and postsynaptic activity. In rate-based terms, coactive neurons strengthen connections; in spike timing terms, a causal order (pre→post within a window) potentiates synapses, whereas the reverse induces depression. This implements a local, biologically plausible form of credit assignment: synapses that drive postsynaptic spikes are strengthened, and those that are driven without eliciting postsynaptic output are weakened. However, without additional circuitry or local signals, pure Hebbian timing rules cannot distinguish neuron-specific contributions to a global error, nor can they prevent runaway potentiation when many inputs co-activate a neuron. <cite id="97c64844-0">Classic Hebbian models face the sign problem: plasticity depends primarily on postsynaptic activity, yet complex functions require fine-grained sign control akin to backprop; circuit motifs can bridge this gap</cite><cite id="4698068d-3">Hebbian STDP is potentiation for postsynaptic spike following presynaptic spike and depression otherwise, and BCM-type models provide a widely supported framework for developing task-selective cells</cite>.

# Mechanism 1: Circuit Scaffolds that Endow Hebbian Rules with Error Sign

Biological microcircuits can encode neuron-specific error signals and deliver them locally to synapses through inhibition and dis-inhibition. In a feedback-driven control-theoretic framework (Deep Feedback Control), top-down feedback targeting inhibitory interneurons produces a dis-inhibitory drive to excitatory neurons; when Hebbian plasticity depends on recurrent inhibition, the net plasticity becomes error-modulated at the circuit level. This yields sign control for each neuron independent of global cost gradients, stabilizes otherwise divergent Hebbian growth, and achieves performance comparable to backprop on deep vision tasks. <cite id="97c64844-0">Assuming errors are encoded in top-down dis-inhibitory afferents and recurrent inhibition influences plasticity, error-modulated learning emerges naturally at the circuit level and matches backprop on nonlinearly separable benchmarks</cite><cite id="97c64844-2">a Hebbian rule with inhibition dependence decodes credit signals from a dis-inhibitory motif, stabilizes runaway Hebbian plasticity, resembles experimental phenomenology, and performs comparably to BP</cite><cite id="97c64844-4">top-down feedback targets excitatory neurons and disinhibitory circuits, providing a substrate for neuron-specific local error signals to modulate the sign of plasticity</cite>.

Operationally, this implements error-correcting credit assignment by:
- Locally identifying which excitatory inputs (or which inhibitory pathways) causally contribute to a neuron’s residual error through dis-inhibitory feedback patterns.
- Using inhibitory synaptic weights within a Hebbian rule to weight the sign of plasticity, so that over-activity or miscausal inputs are downweighted while corrective inputs are potentiated, without requiring global error broadcasts. <cite id="97c64844-0">Inhibition-dependent Hebbian learning maps dis-inhibitory feedback to plasticity sign, resolving discrepancies between functional backprop-like needs and purely phenomenological Hebbian rules</cite><cite id="97c64844-2">the same rule accounts for observed plasticity without inhibition and performs comparably to backprop on multiple benchmarks</cite>.

# Mechanism 2: Local Error Proxies via BCM Dynamics, Predictive Coding, and Two-Phase Contrastive Hebbian Learning

Even without explicit error backpropagation, neurons can compute local proxies for error through feedback and threshold dynamics. BCM rules update synaptic strengths with a sliding threshold that depends on the postsynaptic neuron’s activity history, making weight changes sensitive to the difference between ongoing input statistics and a learned target, i.e., a local error-like signal. Predictive coding networks implement a complementary decomposition: a single Hebbian modification driven by an explicit local error term simplifies plasticity and avoids mistaken updates when targets are absent. In hierarchical autoencoder/predictive-coding architectures, error terms are decomposed into target- and prediction-based components, enabling local Hebbian-like rules that closely track backprop while remaining biologically plausible. <cite id="4698068d-3">A correlation-based Hebbian learning rule stabilizes input–output correlations in spiking neurons, and BCM-style learning underlies orientation selectivity with strong experimental support</cite><cite id="97c64844-3">predictive coding adds explicit error nodes that simplify plasticity to a single Hebbian modification, and related two-phase (contrastive) Hebbian approximations minimize an energy function, achieving good MNIST performance</cite>.

These mechanisms implement error-correcting credit assignment by:
- Continuously correcting synaptic efficacy toward input–response targets through local activity differences (BCM threshold dynamics) or explicit local errors (predictive coding).
- Using local feedback to distinguish target-directed from confounding inputs, thus “correcting” misattributed credit in a feedforward hierarchy without global gradients. <cite id="4698068d-3">BCM-style models provide a biologically grounded way to compute local error proxies via threshold dynamics that shape synaptic changes toward target statistics</cite><cite id="97c64844-3">decomposing errors into target- and predicted-value terms yields single Hebbian updates that remain robust when target information is absent</cite>.

# Mechanism 3: Correlational Robustness and Noise as an Adaptive Correction Signal

A key “error-correction” property of Hebbian/STDP is robustness to noise, especially when spikes encode information efficiently and correlations are managed. Spike-based transmission is intrinsically robust to uncertainty and can admit sparse, low-energy representations; under appropriate conditions, background synaptic activity can enhance discriminability and even relax stability constraints of Hebbian mechanisms, allowing networks to maintain functional connectivity despite internal noise. At the same time, structured background activity can promote distinction among similar inputs, counteracting ambiguity and improving credit assignment fidelity. <cite id="70553646-0">Spike-based encoding with Hebbian/STDP is robust to noise; synaptic background activity can promote distinguishing very similar inputs, and strict stability conditions of Hebbian mechanisms can be relaxed by introducing random external noise</cite><cite id="70553646-4">Hebbian-like adaptation induced by external random noise leads to diverse network structures (including scale-free small-world), indicating an interplay of noise and plasticity that may explain roles of noise in nervous system function</cite>.

# Summary

Hebbian plasticity implements credit assignment by adjusting synapses based on local correlations between presynaptic and postsynaptic activity, most concretely through spike-timing–dependent plasticity (STDP) that potentiates aligned spike pairs and depresses reverse-aligned ones. In biological networks, the sign and specificity of these updates are “error-corrected” by recurrent and feedback microcircuits that encode neuron-specific credit signals (e.g., top-down disinhibition or inhibitory gating), by local error proxies computed from activity differences (e.g., BCM-style threshold dynamics or predictive coding decompositions), and by the statistics of background noise that stabilize or steer correlations. # From Correlation Rules to Credit Assignment: Why Sign and Locality Matter

Hebbian plasticity is defined by changes that depend on the temporal correlations of pre- and postsynaptic activity. In rate-based terms, coactive neurons strengthen connections; in spike timing terms, a causal order (pre→post within a window) potentiates synapses, whereas the reverse induces depression. This implements a local, biologically plausible form of credit assignment: synapses that drive postsynaptic spikes are strengthened, and those that are driven without eliciting postsynaptic output are weakened. However, without additional circuitry or local signals, pure Hebbian timing rules cannot distinguish neuron-specific contributions to a global error, nor can they prevent runaway potentiation when many inputs co-activate a neuron. <cite id="97c64844-0">Classic Hebbian models face the sign problem: plasticity depends primarily on postsynaptic activity, yet complex functions require fine-grained sign control akin to backprop; circuit motifs can bridge this gap</cite><cite id="4698068d-3">Hebbian STDP is potentiation for postsynaptic spike following presynaptic spike and depression otherwise, and BCM-type models provide a widely supported framework for developing task-selective cells</cite>.

# Mechanism 1: Circuit Scaffolds that Endow Hebbian Rules with Error Sign

Biological microcircuits can encode neuron-specific error signals and deliver them locally to synapses through inhibition and dis-inhibition. In a feedback-driven control-theoretic framework (Deep Feedback Control), top-down feedback targeting inhibitory interneurons produces a dis-inhibitory drive to excitatory neurons; when Hebbian plasticity depends on recurrent inhibition, the net plasticity becomes error-modulated at the circuit level. Operationally, this implements error-correcting credit assignment by:
- Locally identifying which excitatory inputs (or which inhibitory pathways) causally contribute to a neuron’s residual error through dis-inhibitory feedback patterns.
- Using inhibitory synaptic weights within a Hebbian rule to weight the sign of plasticity, so that over-activity or miscausal inputs are downweighted while corrective inputs are potentiated, without requiring global error broadcasts. <cite id="97c64844-0">Inhibition-dependent Hebbian learning maps dis-inhibitory feedback to plasticity sign, resolving discrepancies between functional backprop-like needs and purely phenomenological Hebbian rules</cite><cite id="97c64844-2">the same rule accounts for observed plasticity without inhibition and performs comparably to backprop on multiple benchmarks</cite>.

# Mechanism 2: Local Error Proxies via BCM Dynamics, Predictive Coding, and Two-Phase Contrastive Hebbian Learning

Even without explicit error backpropagation, neurons can compute local proxies for error through feedback and threshold dynamics. BCM rules update synaptic strengths with a sliding threshold that depends on the postsynaptic neuron’s activity history, making weight changes sensitive to the difference between ongoing input statistics and a learned target, i.e., a local error-like signal. Predictive coding networks implement a complementary decomposition: a single Hebbian modification driven by an explicit local error term simplifies plasticity and avoids mistaken updates when targets are absent. These mechanisms implement error-correcting credit assignment by:
- Continuously correcting synaptic efficacy toward input–response targets through local activity differences (BCM threshold dynamics) or explicit local errors (predictive coding).

# Mechanism 3: Correlational Robustness and Noise as an Adaptive Correction Signal

A key “error-correction” property of Hebbian/STDP is robustness to noise, especially when spikes encode information efficiently and correlations are managed. Spike-based transmission is intrinsically robust to uncertainty and can admit sparse, low-energy representations; under appropriate conditions, background synaptic activity can enhance discriminability and even relax stability constraints of Hebbian mechanisms, allowing networks to maintain functional connectivity despite internal noise. At the same time, structured background activity can promote distinction among similar inputs, counteracting ambiguity and improving credit assignment fidelity. <cite id="70553646-0">Spike-based encoding with Hebbian/STDP is robust to noise; synaptic background activity can promote distinguishing very similar inputs, and strict stability conditions of Hebbian mechanisms can be relaxed by introducing random external noise</cite><cite id="70553646-4">Hebbian-like adaptation induced by external random noise leads to diverse network structures (including scale-free small-world), indicating an interplay of noise and plasticity that may explain roles of noise in nervous system function</cite>.

Pragmatically, this implements error-correcting credit assignment by:
- Filtering out noncausal correlations via short timing windows and local activity contrasts, so that noise-driven co-activity does not arbitrarily potentiate synapses.
- Leveraging background variability to disambiguate overlapping features, thereby reducing miscredit assignment due to confounded inputs. <cite id="4698068d-3">Hebbian/anti-Hebbian variants and spike timing windows address cases where spike trains invalidate simple pre→post labeling, emphasizing causal ordering for credit assignment</cite><cite id="70553646-0">random background activity can promote discrimination and relax competition constraints, improving robustness of Hebbian mechanisms</cite>.

Experimental support for Hebbian plasticity is broad across brain areas, and modeling shows that with appropriate microcircuit scaffolds, Hebbian-like rules can approximate backprop and learn complex hierarchies. Dis-inhibitory feedback provides neuron-specific local error signs that set the sign of plasticity, while inhibition’s effect on excitatory synapses naturally implements sign control without global error backpropagation. BCM-style local error proxies and predictive coding decompositions appear in neuromorphic and brain-inspired architectures, linking spiking Hebbian updates to gradient-like corrections. # Takeaway

Hebbian plasticity implements error-correcting credit assignment by combining local spike-timing correlations with circuit-level scaffolds and local error proxies. Title: Dis-inhibitory neuronal circuits can control the sign of synaptic plasticity
Snippet: How neuronal circuits achieve credit assignment remains a central unsolved question in systems neuroscience. Various studies have suggested plausible solutions for back-propagating error signals through multi-layer networks. These purely functionally motivated models assume distinct neuronal compartments to represent local error signals that determine the sign of synaptic plasticity. However, this explicit error modulation is inconsistent with phenomenological plasticity models in which the sign depends primarily on postsynaptic activity. Here we show how a plausible microcircuit model and Hebbian learning rule derived within an adaptive control theory framework can resolve this discrepancy. Assuming errors are encoded in top-down dis-inhibitory synaptic afferents, we show that error-modulated learning emerges naturally at the circuit level when recurrent inhibition explicitly influences Hebbian plasticity. The same learning rule accounts for experimentally observed plasticity in the absence of inhibition and performs comparably to back-propagation of error (BP) on several non-linearly separable benchmarks. Our findings bridge the gap between functional and experimentally observed plasticity rules and make concrete predictions on inhibitory modulation of excitatory plasticity.

Title: A Review of Neuroscience-Inspired Machine Learning
Snippet: One of the key tasks in artificial intelligence is to construct mathematical and algorithmic solutions to what is known as the grand problem of credit assignment.Effective credit assignment reduces to: (i) the identification of which neural processing elements (NPEs), e.g., individual computational units in a computation graph, have an influence on a particular (task-specific) objective functional L(Θ); and (ii) modifying the synapses that connect all of the NPEs based on their degree of influence so as to optimize this objective.The synaptic adjustments that characterize the second step are made to improve the overall performance of the network that the set of NPEs constitutes.From the perspective of error-driven learning and adaptation, credit assignment is typically carried out by computing and assigning error values to each NPE based on the cost L(Θ) and, once these values have been obtained, yielding ∆ (the set of all adjustments to be made to the synapses within Θ), the current values of the ANN's parameters are consequently updated.

Note that, historically, error-driven adjustment of the kind described above has been theorized [59,13] and experimentally observed in biological neuronal networks [75].The problem with how this error is computed and allocated in modern-day ANNs -via backpropagation of errors [32] (backprop) -is essentially what is considered to be neurobiologically implausible.Given the significant successes of modern deep learning, addressing this implausibility may seem a niche task of interest to neuroscientists alone.However, this is far from true; despite recent breakthroughs, important advancements are still required.Two of these include the need to: 1) develop more ro-bust and more general human-like capabilities, in service of the grander goal of constructing intelligent machines, and 2) to construct faster, more energy efficient procedures for training and conducting inference in such models.Biologically-plausible credit assignment approaches offer a potential solution to both of these problems.

Biologically-plausible (bio-plausible) credit assignment is suitable for neuromorphic hardware implementations due to the locality of their operations and synaptic updates.

Title: Dis-inhibitory neuronal circuits can control the sign of synaptic plasticity
Snippet: Our main contributions are: 

• We extend Deep Feedback Control (DFC), a recent adaptive control theory framework for error-based learning [24], to a biologically plausible dis-inhibitory microcircuit motif. • We show how a Hebbian plasticity rule with an explicit inhibition dependence can naturally decode credit signals from this microcircuit. • We demonstrate that this rule enables error-based learning in hierarchical networks, naturally stabilizes runaway Hebbian plasticity, and resembles phenomenological plasticity rules under simulated experimental conditions. • Finally, we demonstrate that our learning rule performs comparable to BP in deep neural networks trained on computer vision benchmarks.

Title: An Approximation of the Error Backpropagation Algorithm in a Predictive Coding Network with Local Hebbian Synaptic Plasticity
Snippet: In the above GeneRec model, the error terms δ are not explicitly represented in neural activity, and instead the weight change based on errors is decomposed into a difference of two weight modifications: one based on target value and one based on predicted value. By contrast, the predictive coding model includes additional nodes explicitly representing error and, thanks to them, has a simpler plasticity rule involving just a single Hebbian modification. A potential advantage of such a single modification is robustness to uncertainty about the presence of s out because no mistaken weight updates can be made when s out is not present. 

Bengio and colleagues (Bengio, 2014;Bengio et al., 2015) considered how the backpropagation algorithm can be approximated in a hierarchical network of autoencoders that learn to predict their own inputs. The general frameworks of autoencoders and predictive coding are closely related, as both of the networks, which include feedforward and feedback connections, learn to predict activity on lower levels from the representation on the higher levels. This work (Bengio, 2014;Bengio et al., 2015) includes many Europe PMC Funders Author Manuscripts Europe PMC Funders Author Manuscripts interesting results, such as improvement of learning due to the addition of noise to the system. However, it was not described how it is mapped on a network of simple nodes performing local computation. There is a discussion of a possible plasticity rule at the end of Bengio (2014) that has a similar form as equation 4.2 of the GeneRec model. 

Bengio and colleagues (Scellier & Bengio, 2016;Bengio & Fischer, 2015) introduce another interesting approximation to implement backpropagation in biological neural networks. It has some similarities to the model presented here in that it minimizes an energy function. However, like contrastive Hebbian learning, it operates in two phases, a positive and a negative phase, where weights are updated from information obtained from each phase. The weights are changed following a differential equation update starting at the end of the negative phase and until convergence of the positive phase. Learning must be inhibited during the negative phase, which would require a global signal. This model also achieves good results on the MNIST data set.

Title: Dis-inhibitory neuronal circuits can control the sign of synaptic plasticity
Snippet: How do neurons far away from the sensory periphery and motor output system update their connections to contribute to network computation meaningfully? This question, formally known as the "credit assignment problem," is one of the outstanding questions in systems neuroscience. Classic learning theories assume synaptic plasticity in the brain is mainly Hebbian, i.e., changes in a synapse's efficacy depend merely on the pre-and postsynaptic activity of the neurons it connects [1]. A plethora of experiments in different brain areas support the notion of Hebbian plasticity [2,3] and diverse phenomenological plasticity models quantitatively capture observed synaptic plasticity dynamics [4][5][6][7][8]. Theories of reinforcement learning suggested further extensions of Hebbian learning to three-factor rules that account for reward modulation, whereby a global modulatory factor, e.g., dopamine, explicitly influences the sign of plasticity [9,10]. Again, there is ample experimental evidence for the role of neuromodulators in gating plasticity in various brain areas [11,12]. Yet, recent work argues that global neuromodulation is insufficient to learn complex function mappings in large networks [13,14] and that more fine-grained control over the sign of plasticity is required, as in the BP algorithm used in deep learning [15][16][17][18]. This realization motivated several modeling studies on how biological networks could approximate BP [19][20][21][22][23][24][25]. One central assumption in virtually all of these models is that the sign of plasticity is explicitly modulated by a neuron-specific local error signal akin to the gradient-based update used in BP [26]. However, learning rules with explicit error In neuronal circuits, top-down feedback connections target excitatory neurons, as well as inhibitory and dis-inhibitory circuits that have been implicated in gating of plasticity.
